Here he teaches that it is a greater good to have our names written in heaven than to enjoy the greatest temporal power, even authority over the devils themselves.
The Bible everywhere teaches that in all our conduct eternal good is to be preferred to temporal good.
But this is very different from maintaining that our own individual eternal interest is to be aimed at as the supreme object of regard.
4. The proposition is not that hope and fear should not influence our conduct.

All that is implied is that when we are influenced by hope and fear, the things that are hoped for or feared should be put into the scale according to their real value, in comparison with other interests.

5. The question is not whether those persons did right who are spoken of in the Bible as having been, at least in some degree, influenced by hope and fear, or as having respect to the recompense of the reward, or to the joy that was set before them.
This is admitted. Noah was moved with fear and built the ark.
But was it the fear of being drowned himself, or fear for his own personal safety, that chiefly moved him?
The Bible does not say so.
He feared for the safety of his family; yes, more, he dreaded the destruction of the whole human race, with all the interests depending on it.
Whenever it is said that good men were influenced by hope and fear, it is admitted.
But in order to make it bear on this subject, it must be shown that this hope or fear regarding their own personal interest was the controlling motive.
Now, this is nowhere affirmed in the Bible.
It was right for them to be influenced by promises and threats.
Otherwise, they could not obey the second part of the law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

blocks.x: II. I am to show what is meant by the proposition that a supreme regard for our own interest is inconsistent with true religion.

s: The question is whether a supreme regard for our own happiness is religion.
It is whether we are to fear our own damnation more than the damnation of all other men, and the dishonor done to God by it.
And whether we are to aim at securing our own happiness more than the happiness of all other men and the glory of God.
And whether, if we do this, we act according to the requirements of true religion, or inconsistently with true religion.
This is the proper point of inquiry, and I wish you to keep it constantly in mind, and not to confuse it with any of the other points that I have referred to.

blocks.x: III. Now for the proof of the proposition.

s: Before proceeding to the proof of the proposition that a supreme regard for our own happiness is inconsistent with true religion, I will observe that all true religion consists in being like God: in acting on the same principles and grounds, and having the same feelings toward different objects.
I suppose this will not be denied.
Indeed, it cannot be, by any sane mind.
I then observe, as the first proof of the proposition,
1. That a supreme regard for our own happiness is not according to the example of God, but is being totally unlike him.
The Bible tells us that “God is love.”
That is, benevolence is the sum total of his character.
All his other moral attributes, such as justice, mercy, and the like, are only modifications of this benevolence.
His love is shown in two forms.
One is that of benevolence: willing good, or desiring the happiness of others.
The other is delight, or approval of the character of others who are holy.
God’s benevolence regards all beings that are capable of happiness.
This is universal. Toward all holy beings he exercises the love of delight. In other words, God loves his neighbor as himself.
He regards the interests of all beings, according to their relative value, as much as his own.
He seeks his own happiness, or glory, as the supreme good.
But not because it is his own, but because it is the supreme good.
The sum total of his happiness, as an infinite being, is infinitely greater than the sum total of the happiness of all other beings, or of any possible number of finite creatures.
Take a very familiar illustration.
Here is a man who is kind to animals.
This man and his horse fall into the river.
Now, does true benevolence require the man to drown himself in order to rescue his horse?
No. It would be true disinterested benevolence in him to save himself and, if need be, leave his horse to perish, because his happiness is of so much greater value than that of the horse.
You see this at a glance.
But the difference between God and all created beings is infinitely greater than that between a man and a horse, or between the highest angel and the lowliest insect.
God, therefore, regards the happiness of all creatures precisely according to its real value.
And unless we do the same, we are not like God.
If we are like God, we must regard God’s happiness and glory in the same light that he does; that is, as the supreme good, beyond everything else in the universe.
And if we desire our own happiness more than God’s happiness, we are infinitely unlike God.
2. To aim at our own happiness supremely is inconsistent with true religion, because it is contrary to the spirit of Christ.
We are told that “if any man does not have the spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.”
And it is repeatedly said of him, as a man, that he did not seek his own, that he did not seek his own glory, and the like.
What was he seeking?
Was it his own personal salvation?
No. Was it his own personal happiness?
No. It was the glory of his Father and the good of the universe, through the salvation of men.
He came on an errand of pure benevolence, to benefit the kingdom of God, not to benefit himself.
This was “the joy that was set before him,” for which “he endured the cross, despising the shame.”
It was the great good he could do by thus giving himself up to labor and suffer for the salvation of men.
3. To regard our own happiness as the supreme object of pursuit is contrary to the law of God.
I have mentioned this before, but I return to it again for the sake of making my present demonstration complete.

The sum of that law is this: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
This is the great thing required: benevolence toward God and man.
The first thing is truly to love the happiness and glory of God above all other things, because it is so infinitely lovely and desirable, and is properly the supreme good.
Some have objected that it is not our duty to seek the happiness of God, because his happiness is already secured.

Suppose, now, that the king of England is perfectly independent of me, and has his happiness secured without me; does that make it any less my duty to wish him well, to desire his happiness, and to rejoice in it?
Because God is happy in himself, independent of his creatures, is that a reason why we should not love his happiness and rejoice in it? Strange!
Again: we are bound by the terms of God’s law to take delight in God, because he is holy, infinitely holy.

Again: this law binds us to exercise the same good will, or benevolence, toward others that we exercise toward ourselves; that is, to seek both their interests and our own, according to their relative value.
Which of you is doing this?
And we are bound to exercise the love of delight toward those who are good and holy.
Thus we see that the sum of the law of God is to exercise benevolence toward God and all beings, according to their relative value, and delight in all who are holy.
Now I say that to regard our own happiness supremely, or to seek it as our supreme end, is contrary to that law, both to its letter and to its spirit. And
4. It is as contrary to the gospel as it is to the law.
In the chapter from which the text is taken, the apostle begins, “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and do not have charity, I have become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and do not have charity, I am nothing.”
Charity here means love.
In the original it is the same word that is translated love.
“And though I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and do not have charity, it profits me nothing.”
Now, take note! He could not have expressed in stronger language the idea that charity, or benevolence, is essential to true religion.
See how he sets up his guards on every side, so that it is impossible to mistake his views.
If a person does not have true charity, he is nothing.
He then goes on to show what the characteristics of this true charity are.

“Charity suffers long, and is kind; charity does not envy; charity does not boast of itself, is not puffed up, does not behave itself improperly, does not seek her own, is not easily provoked, thinks no evil; does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.”
Here you see that one leading characteristic of this love is that charity “does not seek her own.”
Mark that! If this is true religion, and without it there is no religion, then one characteristic of true religion is that it “does not seek her own.”
Those of you who have Bibles with marginal references can follow out these references and find a multitude of passages that plainly teach the same thing.
Remember the passages I quoted in the last lecture.
I will refer to just one of them: “Whoever would save his life shall lose it.”
Here you see it laid down as an established principle of God’s government that if a person aims supremely at his own interest, he will lose his own interest.
The same is taught in the tenth chapter of this epistle, verse 24: “Let no man seek his own, but every man another’s wealth.”
If you look at the passage, you will see that the word wealth is in italics, to show that it was a word added by the translators, one that is not in the Greek.
They might just as well have used the word happiness, or welfare, as wealth.
So also in the 33rd verse: “Even as I please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved.”
Therefore I say that to make our own interest the supreme object of pursuit is as contrary to the gospel as it is to the law.
5. It is contrary to conscience.
The universal conscience of mankind has decided that a supreme regard for our own happiness is not virtue.
Men have always known that to serve God and benefit mankind is what is right, and that to seek their own personal interest supremely is not right.

They have always regarded it as mean and contemptible for individuals to seek their own happiness as the supreme object; and consequently we see how much pains men take to conceal their selfishness and to appear benevolent.

It is impossible for any man, unless his conscience is strangely dulled by sin or perverted by false instruction, not to see that it is sinful to regard his own happiness above other interests of greater importance.
6. It is contrary to right reason.
Right reason teaches us to regard all things according to their real value.
God does this, and we should do the same.
God has given us reason for this very purpose, that we should weigh and compare the relative value of things.
It is a mockery of reason to deny that it teaches us to regard things according to their real value.
And if so, then to aim at and prefer our own interest as the supreme end is contrary to reason.
7. It is contrary to common sense.
What has the common sense of mankind decided on this point?
Look at the common sense of mankind in regard to what is called patriotism.
No man was ever regarded as a true patriot in fighting for his country if his object was to serve his own interest.
Suppose it should appear that his object in fighting was to get himself crowned king; would anybody give him credit for patriotism?
No. All men agree that it is patriotism when a man is disinterested, like Washington, and fights for his country for his country’s sake.
The common sense of mankind has stamped its condemnation on that spirit which seeks its own things and prefers its own interests to the greater interests of others.
It is evident that all men regard it so.
Otherwise, how is it that everyone is anxious to appear disinterested?
8. It is contrary to the constitution of the mind.
I do not mean by this that it is impossible, by our very constitution, for us to seek our own happiness as the supreme object.
But we are so constituted that if we do this, we can never attain it.
As I have said in a former lecture, happiness is the gratification of desire.
We must desire something, and gain the object we desire.
Now, suppose a man desires his own happiness: the object of his desire will always stay just so far ahead of him, like his shadow, and the faster he pursues it, the faster it flies.
Happiness is inseparably attached to the attainment of the object desired.
Suppose I desire a thousand dollars.
That is the thing on which my desire fastens, and when I get it, that desire is gratified, and I am happy, so far as gratifying this desire goes toward making me happy.
But if I desire the thousand dollars for the purpose of getting a watch, a suit of clothes, and such things, the desire is not gratified until I get those things.
But now suppose the thing I desired was my own happiness.
Then getting the thousand dollars does not make me happy, because that is not the thing my desire was fixed on.
And so getting the watch, and the clothes, and other things will not make me happy, for they do not gratify my desire.
God has so constituted things, and given such laws to the mind, that man can never gain happiness by pursuing it.
This very constitution plainly indicates the duty of disinterested benevolence.
Indeed, he has made it impossible for men to be happy except in proportion as they are disinterested.
Here are two men walking along the street together.
They come across a man who has just been run over by a cart and lies weltering in his blood.
They pick him up, carry him to the surgeon, and relieve him.
Now it is plain that their gratification is in proportion to the intensity of their desire for his relief.
If one of them felt but little and cared but little about the sufferings of the poor man, he will be gratified but little.
But if his desire to have the man relieved amounted to agony, his gratification would be in keeping with it.
Now suppose a third individual who had no desire to relieve the distressed man; certainly relieving him could be no gratification to that person.
He could pass right by him and see him die.
Then he is not gratified at all.
Therefore, you see, happiness is just in proportion as the desires are gratified by obtaining the things desired.
Observe here that in order to make the happiness of gratified desire complete, the desire itself must be virtuous.
Otherwise, if the desire is selfish, the gratification will be mingled with pain from the conflict of the mind.
That all this is true is a matter of consciousness, and is proved to us by the very highest kind of testimony we can have.
And for anyone to deny it is to charge God with folly, as if he had given us a constitution that would not allow us to be happy in obeying him.
9. It is also inconsistent with our own happiness to make our own interest the supreme object.
This follows from what I have just said.
Men may enjoy a certain kind of pleasure, but not true happiness.
The pleasure which does not spring from the gratification of virtuous desire is a deceptive delusion.
The reason why all mankind do not find happiness, when they are all so anxious for it, is that they are seeking IT.
If they would seek the glory of God and the good of the universe as their supreme end, IT would pursue them.
10. It is inconsistent with the public happiness.

If each individual is to aim at his own happiness as his chief end, these interests will unavoidably clash and come into collision, and universal war and confusion will follow in the train of universal selfishness.
11. To maintain that a supreme regard for our own interest is true religion is to contradict the experience of all real saints.
I affirm that every real saint knows that his supreme happiness consists in going out of himself, and in regarding the glory of God and the good of others.
If he does not know this, he is no saint.
12. It is also inconsistent with the experience of all those who have had a selfish religion, and have found out their mistake and obtained true religion.
This is a common occurrence.
I suppose I have known hundreds of cases.
Some members of this church have recently made this discovery.
And they can all testify that they now know by experience that benevolence is true religion.
13. It is contrary to the experience of all the impenitent.
Every impenitent sinner knows that he is aiming supremely at the promotion of his own interest, and he knows that he does not have true religion.
The very thing for which his conscience condemns him is this, that he is regarding his own interest instead of the glory of God.
Now just turn the page over for a moment, and admit that a supreme regard for our own happiness is true religion; and then see what will follow.
1. Then it will follow that God is not holy.
That is, if a supreme regard for our own interest, because it is our own, is true religion, then it will follow that God is not holy.
God regards his own happiness, but that is because it is the greatest good, not because it is his own.
But he is love, or benevolence; and if benevolence is not true religion, God’s nature must be changed.
2. The law of God must be altered.

If a supreme regard for our own happiness is religion, then the law should read, “You shall love yourself with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength, and God and your neighbor infinitely less than yourself.”
3. The gospel must be reversed.
Instead of saying, “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God,” it should read, “Do all for your own happiness.”

Instead of “He who would save his life shall lose it,” we should find it saying, “He who is supremely anxious to save his own life shall save it; but he who is benevolent, and willing to lose his life for the good of others, shall lose it.”
4. The consciences of men would have to be changed so as to testify in favor of selfishness, and to condemn and reject everything like disinterested benevolence.
5. Right reason must be made not to weigh things according to their relative value, but to judge our own little interest to be of more value than the greatest interests of God and the universe.
6. Common sense will have to decide that true patriotism consists in every man’s seeking his own interest instead of the public good, and each one seeking to build himself up as high as he can.
7. The human constitution must be reversed.
If supreme selfishness is virtue, the human constitution was made wrong.
It is so made that man can be happy only by being benevolent.
And if this doctrine is true, that religion consists in seeking our own happiness as a supreme good, then the more religion a man has, the more miserable he is.
8. And the whole framework of society will have to be changed.
As it now stands, the good of the community depends on the extent to which everyone regards the public interest.
And if this doctrine holds, it must be changed, so that the public good will be best promoted when every man is scrambling for his own interest regardless of the interests of others.
9. The experience of the saints will have to be reversed.

Instead of finding, as they now do, that the more benevolence they have, the more religion and the more happiness they have, they should testify that the more they aim at their own good, the more they enjoy of religion and of the favor of God.
10. The impenitent should be found to testify that they are supremely happy in supreme selfishness, and that they find true happiness in it.
I will not pursue this proof any further; it would look like trifling.
If there is any such thing as proof to be had, it is fully proved that to aim at our own happiness supremely is inconsistent with true religion.

blocks.x: REMARKS.

s: I. We see why it is that while all are pursuing happiness, so few find it.
The fact is plain.
The reason is this: the greater part of mankind do not know what true happiness consists in, and they are seeking it in that which can never provide it.
They do not find it because they are pursuing it.
If they would turn around and pursue holiness, happiness would pursue them.
If they would become disinterested, and devote themselves to doing good, they could not help but be happy.
If they choose happiness as an end, it flies before them.
True happiness consists in the gratification of virtuous desires; and if they would set themselves to glorify God and do good, they would find it.
The only class of persons who never find it, in this world or in the world to come, are those who seek it as an end.
II. The constitution of the human mind and of the universe affords a beautiful illustration of the economy of God.
Suppose man could find happiness only by pursuing his own happiness.

Then each individual would have only the happiness that he himself had gained, and all the happiness in the universe would be only the sum total of what individuals had gained, offset by all the pain and misery produced by conflicting interests.
Now take note! God has so constituted things that while each one devotes himself to promoting the happiness of others, his own happiness is secured and made complete.
How vastly greater, then, is the amount of happiness in the universe than it would have been had selfishness been the law of Jehovah’s kingdom!
For each one who obeys the law of God fully secures his own happiness by his benevolence, and the happiness of the whole is increased by as much as each receives from all the others.
Many say, “Who will take care of my happiness if I do not?
If I am to care only for my neighbor’s interest and neglect my own, none of us will be happy.”
That would be true if your care for your neighbor’s happiness took away from your own.
But if your happiness consists in doing good and promoting the happiness of others, then the more you do for others, the more you promote your own happiness.
III. When I announced the subject of this lecture, I avoided using the term selfishness, for fear that it would be thought invidious.
But I now affirm that a supreme regard for our own interest is selfishness, and nothing else.
It would be selfishness in God if he regarded his own interest supremely because it is his own.
And it is selfishness in man.
And whoever maintains that a supreme regard for our own interest is true religion maintains that selfishness is true religion.
IV. If selfishness is virtue, then benevolence is sin.
They are direct opposites and cannot both be virtue.
For a man to set up his own interest over God’s interest, giving it preference and placing it in opposition to God’s interest, is selfishness.
And if this is virtue, then Jesus Christ, in seeking the good of mankind as he did, departed from the principles of virtue.
Who will claim this?
V. Those who regard their own interest as supreme, and yet think they have true religion, are deceived.
I say it solemnly, because I believe it is true, and I would say it if it were the last word I was to speak before going to the judgment.
Dear hearer, whoever you are, if you are doing this, you are not a Christian.
Do not call this being censorious.
I am not censorious.
I would not denounce anyone.
But as God is true, and as your soul is going to the judgment, you do not have the religion of the Bible.
VI. Some will ask here, “What! Are we to have no regard for our happiness? And if so, how are we to decide whether it is supreme or not?”
I do not say that.
I say you may regard it according to its relative value.
And now I ask, is there any real practical difficulty here?
I appeal to your consciousness.
You cannot help but know, if you are honest, what it is that you regard supremely.
Are these interests, your own interest on one side, and God’s glory and the good of the universe on the other, so nearly balanced in your mind that you cannot tell which you prefer?
It is impossible! If you are not as conscious that you prefer the glory of God to your own interest as you are that you exist, you may take it for granted that you are all wrong.
VII. You see why the enjoyment of so many who profess religion depends on their evidences.
These persons are hunting after evidence all the time; and just in proportion as that varies, their enjoyment waxes and wanes.
Now, take note! If they really regarded the glory of God and the good of mankind, their enjoyment would not depend on their evidences.
Those who are purely selfish may enjoy much in religion, but it is by anticipation.
The idea of going to heaven is pleasing to them.
But those who go out of themselves, and are purely benevolent, have a present heaven in their hearts.
VIII. You see here that all of you who had no peace and joy in religion before you had a hope are deceived.
Perhaps I can give an outline of your experience.
You were awakened, and were distressed, as you had reason to be, by the fear of going to hell.
By and by, perhaps while you were engaged in prayer, or while someone was talking with you, your distress left you.
You thought your sins were pardoned.
A gleam of joy shot through your mind and warmed your heart into a glow, which you took for evidence, and this in turn increased your joy.
How very different is the experience of a true Christian!
His peace does not depend on his hope; but true submission and benevolence produce peace and joy, independent of his hope.
Suppose the case of a man in prison, condemned to be hanged the next day.
He is in great distress, pacing his cell and waiting for the day.
By and by a messenger comes with a pardon.
He seizes the paper, turns it up to the dim light that comes through his grate, reads the word PARDON, almost faints with emotion, and leaps for joy.
He supposes the paper to be genuine.
Now suppose it turns out that the paper is counterfeit.
Suddenly his joy is all gone.
So it is in the case of a deceived person.
He was afraid of going to hell, and of course he rejoices if he believes he is pardoned.
If the devil should tell him so, and he believed it, his joy would be just as great, while the belief lasts, as if it were a reality.
True Christian joy does not depend on evidence.
He submits himself into the hands of God with such confidence, and that very act gives him peace.
He had a terrible conflict with God, but all at once he yields the controversy and says, “God will do right; let God’s will be done.”
Then he begins to pray, he is subdued, he melts down before God, and that very act affords sweet, calm, and heavenly joy.
Perhaps he has not thought of a hope.
Perhaps he may go for hours, or even for a day or two, full of joy in God, without thinking of his own salvation.
You ask him if he has a hope; he never thought of that.
His joy does not depend on believing that he is pardoned, but consists in a state of mind that acquiesces in the government of God.
In such a state of mind, he could not help but be happy.
Now let me ask: which religion do you have?

If you exercise true religion, then suppose God should put you into hell, and there let you exercise supreme love to God, and the same love to your neighbor as to yourself; that itself is a state of mind inconsistent with being miserable.
I wish this to be fully understood.
These hope-seekers will always be disappointed.
If you run after hope, you will never have a hope that is worth anything.
But if you pursue holiness, hope and peace and joy will come as a matter of course.
Is your religion the love of holiness, the love of God and of souls?
Or is it only a hope?
IX. You see why it is that anxious sinners do not find peace.
They are looking at their own guilt and danger.
They are regarding God as an avenger, and shrinking from his terrors.
This will make it impossible for them ever to come to peace.
While they are looking at the wrath of God, which makes them wither and tremble, they cannot love him; they hide from him.
Anxious sinners, let me tell you a secret.
If you keep looking at that feature of God’s character, it will drive you to despair, and that is inconsistent with true submission.

You should look at his whole character, and see the reasons why you should love him, and throw yourself upon him without reserve and without distrust; and instead of shrinking from him, come right to him and say, “O Father in heaven, you are not inexorable; you are sovereign, but you are good. I submit to your government, and give myself to you, with all I have and all I am, body and soul, for time and for eternity.”
The subject for the next lecture will be the distinction between legal submission and gospel submission, or between the religion of the law and the religion of faith.
And here let me observe that when I began to preach on the subject of selfishness in religion, I did not dream that anyone would regard it as a controversial subject at all.
I have no fondness for controversy, and I would as soon think of calling the doctrine of the existence of God a controversial subject as this.
The question is one of the greatest importance, and we ought to weigh the arguments and decide according to the word of God.

Soon we shall go together to the bar of God, and you must determine whether you will go there with selfishness in your hearts, or with that disinterested benevolence that does not seek her own. Will you now be honest?
For as God is true, if you are seeking your own, you will soon be in hell, unless you repent.
Oh, be honest! And lay aside prejudice, and act for eternity.
Text: “Love works no ill to its neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.” — Romans 13:10
In speaking from these words, I intend:
I. To make some remarks about the nature of love.
II. To show that love is the whole of religion.
III. Some things that are not essential to perfect love.
IV. Some things that are essential to it.
V. Some of the effects that perfect love produces.

blocks.x: I. I will make some remarks on the nature of love.

s: 1. The first remark I have to make is that love may exist in various forms.
The two principal forms, as far as religion is concerned, are benevolence and delight.
Benevolence is an affection of the mind, that is, an act of the will.
It is willing good, or a desire to promote the happiness of its object.
Delight is esteem, or approval of the character of its object.
Benevolence should be exercised toward all beings, regardless of their moral character.
Delight is due only to the good and holy.
2. Love may exist either as an affection or as an emotion.
When love is an affection, it is voluntary; it consists in the act of the will.
When it is an emotion, it is involuntary.
What we call feelings, or emotions, are involuntary.
They are not directly dependent on the will, nor controlled by a direct act of the will.
The virtue of love is found mostly when it takes the form of an affection.
The happiness of love is found mostly when it takes the form of an emotion.
If the affection of love is very strong, it produces a high degree of happiness; but the emotion of holy love is happiness itself.
I said that the emotion of love is involuntary.
I do not mean that the will has nothing to do with it, but that it is not the result of a mere or direct act of the will.
No one can exercise the emotion of love merely by willing it.
And the emotion may often exist in spite of the will.

People often feel emotions rising in their minds which they know to be improper, and they try by direct efforts of the will to banish them from their minds; and finding that impossible, they conclude that they have no control over these emotions.
But they may always be controlled by the will in an indirect way.
The mind can call up any class of emotions it chooses by directing its attention sufficiently to the proper object.
They are certain to rise in proportion as the attention is fixed, provided the will is right in regard to the object of attention.
So it is with those emotions which are improper or unpleasant: the mind may be rid of them by turning its attention entirely away from the object and not allowing the thoughts to dwell on it.
3. Ordinarily, the emotions of love toward God are experienced when we exercise love toward Him in the form of affection.
But this is not always so.
We may exercise goodwill toward any object and yet at times feel no perceptible emotions of love.
It is not certain that even the Lord Jesus Christ exercised love toward God in the form of emotion at all times.

As far as our acquaintance with the nature of the mind goes, we know that a person may exercise affection, and be guided and governed by it constantly in all his actions, without any felt emotion of love toward its object at the time.

Thus a husband and father may be occupied in laboring for the benefit of his family, with his very life controlled by affection for them, while his thoughts are not so taken up with them as to make him feel any perceptible emotions of love toward them at the time.

The things with which he is occupied may take up his mind so much that he scarcely has a thought of them, and so he may have no felt emotion toward them; and yet all the while he is guided and governed by affection for them.
Observe here that I use the term affection in the sense of President Edwards, as he explains it in his celebrated Treatise on the Will.
An affection, in his treatise, is an act of the will, or a volition.
4. Love to our neighbor naturally implies the existence of love to God, and love to God naturally implies love to our neighbor.
The same thing is declared in the 8th verse: “Owe no man anything, but to love one another; for he that loves another has fulfilled the law.

For this—You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, You shall not covet—and if there is any other commandment, it is briefly contained in this saying, namely, You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Here it is taken for granted that love to our neighbor implies the existence of love to God; otherwise it could not be said that “he that loves another has fulfilled the law.”
The apostle James recognizes the same principle when he says, “If you fulfill the royal law according to the scripture, You shall love your neighbor as yourself, you do well.”
Here love to our neighbor is spoken of as constituting obedience to the whole law.
Benevolence, that is, goodwill to our neighbor, naturally implies love to God.
It is love for the happiness of being.
So the love of delight toward holy beings naturally implies love to God, as a being of infinite holiness.

blocks.x: II. I will show that love is the whole of religion.

s: In other words, all that God requires of man consists in love, in its various modifications and results.
Love is the sum total of all.
1. The first proof I shall offer is that this truth is taught in the text and in many other passages of Scripture.
The Scriptures fully teach that love is the sum total of all the requirements, both of the law and of the gospel.

Our Savior declares that the great commandment—You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength, and your neighbor as yourself—is the sum total of all the law and the prophets; that is, it implies and includes all that the whole Scriptures, the law and the gospel, require.
2. God is love; and to love is to be like God, and to be perfect in love is to be perfect as God is perfect.
All God’s moral attributes consist in love, acting under certain circumstances and for certain ends.
God’s justice in punishing the wicked, His anger at sin, and the like, are only exercises of His love for the general happiness of His kingdom.
So it is in man.
All that is good in man is some modification of love.
Hatred of sin is only love for virtue, acting itself out in opposing whatever is opposed to virtue.
So true faith implies and includes love; and faith which has no love in it, or which does not work by love, is no part of religion.
The faith that belongs to religion is an affectionate confidence in God.
There is a kind of faith in God which has no love in it.
The devil has that kind of faith.
The sinner under conviction has it.
But there is no religion in it.
Faith might rise even to the faith of miracles, and yet if there is no love in it, it amounts to nothing.

The apostle Paul, in the 13th chapter of 1 Corinthians, says, “Though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and do not have charity, I am nothing.”
It is just so with repentance.
The repentance that does not include love is not “repentance toward God.”
True repentance implies obedience to the law of love, and consequent opposition to sin.

blocks.x: III. I will mention some things that are not essential to perfect love.

s: 1. The highest degree of emotion is not essential to perfect love.
It is evident that the Lord Jesus Christ very seldom had the highest degree of the emotion of love, and yet He always had perfect love.
He generally showed very little emotion, or excitement.
Excitement is always proportioned to the strength of the emotions, since it consists in them.
The Savior generally seemed remarkably calm.
Sometimes His indignation was strong, or His grief at the hardness of men’s hearts; and sometimes we read that He rejoiced in spirit.
But He was commonly calm, and showed no high degree of emotion.
And it is plainly not essential to perfect love that the emotion of love should exist in a high degree.
2. Perfect love does not exclude the idea of increase in love, or growth in grace.
I suppose that the growth of the mind in knowledge to all eternity naturally implies growth in love to all eternity.
The Lord Jesus Christ, in His human nature, grew in stature and in favor with God and man.
No doubt, as a child, He grew in knowledge; and as He grew in knowledge, He grew in love toward God, as well as in favor with God.
His love was perfect when He was a child, but it was greater when He became a man.
As a human being, He probably continued to increase in love to God as long as He lived.
From the nature of the mind, we see that it may be so with all the saints in glory: their love will increase to all eternity, and yet it is always perfect love.
3. It is not essential to perfect love that love should always be exercised toward all individuals alike.
We cannot think of all individuals at once.
You cannot even think of every individual among your acquaintances at once.
The degree of love toward an individual depends on whether that individual is present to our thoughts.
4. It is not essential to perfect love that there should be the same degree of the spirit of prayer for every individual, or for the same individual at all times.
The spirit of prayer is not always essential to pure and perfect love.
The saints in heaven have pure and perfect love for all beings, yet we do not know that they have the spirit of prayer for any.
You may love an individual with a very strong degree of love, and yet not have the spirit of prayer for that individual.
That is, the Spirit of God may not lead you to pray for the salvation of that individual.
You do not pray for the wicked in hell.
The spirit of prayer depends on the influences of the Holy Spirit, leading the mind to pray for things agreeable to the will of God.
You cannot pray in the Spirit with the same degree of fervor and faith for all mankind.
Jesus Christ said expressly that He did not pray for all mankind: “It is not for the world that I pray.”
Here there has been a great mistake in regard to the spirit of prayer.
Some suppose that Christians have not done all their duty if they have not prayed in faith for every individual, as long as there is a sinner on earth.
Then Jesus Christ never did all His duty, for He never did this.
God has never told us that He will save all mankind, and has never given us any reason to believe He will do it.
How then can we pray in faith for the salvation of all?
What does that faith have to rest on?
5. Perfect love is not inconsistent with those feelings of languor or bodily weakness which are the necessary consequence of exhaustion or ill health.
We are so made that excitement naturally and necessarily exhausts our powers.
But love may be perfect nevertheless.
Though a person may feel more like lying down and sleeping than like praying, yet his love may be perfect.
The Lord Jesus Christ often felt this weariness and exhaustion, when the spirit was still willing but the flesh was weak.

blocks.x: IV. What is essential to perfect love.

s: 1. It implies that there is nothing in the mind inconsistent with love.
No hatred, malice, wrath, envy, or any other malignant emotions that are inconsistent with pure and perfect love.
2. That there is nothing in the life inconsistent with love.
All the actions, words, and thoughts continually under the entire and perfect control of love.
3. That love to God is supreme.
Love to God is completely supreme, and so entirely above all other objects that nothing else is loved in comparison with God.
4. That love to God is disinterested.
God is loved for what He is; not for His relation to us, but for the excellence of His character.

5. That love to our neighbor should be equal; that is, that his interest and happiness should be regarded by us as of equal value with our own, and that he and his interests are to be treated by us accordingly.

blocks.x: V. I will mention some of the effects of perfect love.

s: 1. One effect of perfect love to God and man will certainly be delight in self-denial for the sake of promoting the interests of God’s kingdom and the salvation of sinners.
See affectionate parents, how they delight in self-denial for the sake of promoting the happiness of their children.

There is a father: he gives himself up to exhausting labor, day after day and year after year, through the whole of a long life, rising early and continually eating the bread of anxious care, to promote the welfare of his family.
And he counts all this self-denial and toil not a grief or a burden, but a delight, because of the love he bears his family.
See that mother: she wishes to educate her son at college.
And now, instead of finding it painful, it is a joy to her to sit up late and labor incessantly to help him.
That is because she truly loves her son.
Such parents rejoice more in bestowing gifts on their children than they would in enjoying the same things themselves.
What parent does not enjoy a piece of fruit more in giving it to his little child than in eating it himself?
The Lord Jesus Christ enjoyed more solid satisfaction in working out salvation for mankind than any of His saints can ever enjoy in receiving favors at His hands.
He testified that it is more blessed to give than to receive.
This was the joy set before Him, for which He endured the cross and despised the shame.
His love for mankind was so great that it compelled Him to undertake this work, and sustained Him triumphantly through it.

The apostle Paul did not count it a grief and a hardship to be hunted from place to place, imprisoned, scourged, stoned, and counted the refuse of all things, for the sake of spreading the gospel and saving souls.
It was his joy.
The love of Christ so compelled him, and he had such a desire to do good, that it was his highest delight to lay himself on that altar as a sacrifice to the cause.
Other individuals have had the same mind as the apostle.

People have been known who would be willing to live a thousand years, or to the end of time, if they could be employed in doing good, in promoting the kingdom of God, and in saving the souls of men, and who were willing to forgo even sleep and food to benefit the objects they so greatly love.
2. It delivers the soul from the power of legal motives.
Perfect love leads a person to obey God, not because he fears the wrath of God, or hopes to be rewarded for doing this or that, but because he loves God and loves to do the will of God.
There are two extremes on this subject.
One class makes virtue consist in doing right simply because it is right, without any reference to the will of God or any influence from love to God.
Another class makes virtue consist in acting from love of the activity itself, but without reference to God’s authority as Ruler and Lawgiver.
Both of these are in error.
To do a thing simply because one thinks it right, and not out of love to God, is not virtue.
Neither is it virtue to do a thing because one loves to do it, with no regard to God’s will.

A woman might do certain things because she knew it would please her husband; but if she did the same thing merely because she loved to do it, and with no regard to her husband, it would be no virtue as far as her husband is concerned.
If a person loves God, as soon as he knows what God’s will is, he will do it because it is God’s will.
Perfect love will lead to universal obedience—to doing God’s will in all things, because it is the will of God.
3. The individual who exercises perfect love will be dead to the world.
By this I mean that he will be cut loose from the influence of worldly considerations.
Perfect love will so annihilate selfishness that he will have no will but the will of God, and no interest but God’s glory.
He will not be influenced by public opinion, or by what this or that man will say or think.
See that woman, what she will do out of natural affection for her husband.

She is willing to cut loose from all her friends, as much as if she were dead to them, and to pay not the least regard to what they say, and to leave all the riches and honors and delights they can offer, in order to join the one she loves and live with him in poverty, in disgrace, and in exile.
Her affection is so great that she does it joyfully, and is ready to go from a palace to any cottage or cave on earth and be perfectly happy.
And all that her friends can say against the man of her affection has not the least influence on her mind, except to make her cling the more closely to him.
This one ALL-ABSORBING affection has actually killed all the influences that used to act on her.
To attempt to influence her by such things is in vain.
There is only one avenue of approach to her mind; only one class of motives moves her, and that is through the object of her affection.
As far as the philosophy of the mind is concerned, the perfect love of God operates in the same way.
It is impossible to divert from God the mind that is filled with perfect love, while that love continues in exercise.

Take away his worldly possessions, his friends, his good name, his children; send him to prison, beat him with stripes, bind him to the stake, fill his flesh full of pine knots and set them on fire; and then leave him his God, and he is happy.
His strong affection can make him insensible to everything else.
He is as if he were dead to all the world but his God.
Cases have been known of martyrs who, while their bodies were frying at the stake, were so perfectly happy in God as to lose the sense of pain.
Put such a one in hell, in the lake of fire and brimstone, and as long as he enjoys God, and the love of God fills his soul, he is happy.
Who has not witnessed or heard of cases of affection approaching in degree what I have described, where a person is in fact dead to all other things and lives only for the loved one?
How often do you see fond parents who live for an only child, and when that child dies, wish themselves dead!
Sometimes a husband and wife have such an absorbing affection for each other that they live for nothing else; and if the husband dies, the wife pines away and dies also.
The soul-absorbing object for which she lived is gone, and why should she live any longer?

So, when an individual is filled with the perfect love of God, he wishes to live only to love and serve God; he is dead to the world, dead to his own reputation, and has no desire to live for any other reason—here, or in heaven, or anywhere else in the universe—but to glorify God.
He is willing to live, here or anywhere else, and to suffer and labor a thousand years, or to all eternity, if it will glorify God.

I recall often hearing a friend say, “I don’t know that I have one thought of living a single moment for any other purpose than to glorify God, any more than I would think of leaping right into hell.”
This was said soberly and deliberately, and the whole life of that individual corresponded with the declaration.
He was intelligent, sober-minded, and honest, and I have no doubt he expressed what had been the fullest conviction of his mind for years.
What was this but perfect love?
What more does any angel in heaven do than this?
His love may be greater in degree, because his strength is greater.
But the highest angel could not love more perfectly than to be able to say in sincerity, “I would as soon think of leaping into hell as of living one moment for any other object but to glorify God.”
What more could Jesus Christ Himself say than that?
4. It is hardly necessary to say that perfect joy and peace are the natural results of perfect love.
But I wish to turn your attention here to what the apostle says in the 13th chapter of 1 Corinthians, speaking of charity, or love.
You will observe that the word here translated charity is the same one that is rendered love in other places.
It means love. “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and do not have charity, I have become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.
And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and do not have charity, I am nothing.”
He might have even the faith of miracles, so strong that he could move mountains from their everlasting foundations, and yet have no love.
“And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and do not have charity, it profits me nothing.”
You see how far he supposes a man may go without love.
“Charity suffers long.” Long-suffering is meekness under opposition or injury.
This is one of the effects of love: to bear great provocations and not retaliate or revile in return.
Love “is kind,” or affectionate in all its dealings with others, never harsh or rude, never needlessly giving pain to anyone.
Love “is not envious”; it never dislikes others because they are more thought of or noticed, more honored or useful, or make greater attainments in knowledge, happiness or piety.
It “is not puffed up” with pride, but is always humble and modest.
It “does not behave itself unbecomingly,” but naturally produces a pleasant and courteous bearing toward all.
However unacquainted with the ways of society the individual who is moved by perfect love may be, he always appears well; it is natural to him to be so kind and gentle and courteous.
It “does not seek its own,” that is, it has no selfishness.
It “is not easily provoked.”
This is always the effect of love.
See that mother, how long she bears with her children, because she loves them.
If you see an individual who is testy or crusty, easily flying into a passion when anything goes wrong, he is by no means perfect in love, if he has any love.
To be easily provoked is always a sign of pride.
If a person is full of love, it is impossible to make him exercise sinful anger while love continues.
He exercises such indignation as God exercises, and as holy angels feel, at what is base and wrong, but he will not be provoked by it.

It “thinks no evil.” Show me a man who is always suspicious of the motives of others, and forever putting the worst construction on the words and actions of his fellow men, and I will show you one who has the devil in him, not the Holy Spirit.
He has that in his own mind which makes him think evil of others.
If an individual is honest and simple-hearted himself, he will be the last to think evil of others.
He will not always be smelling out heresy or mischief in others.
On the contrary, such persons are often liable to be imposed upon by scheming men, not from any lack of good sense, but from the effect of love.
They do not suspect evil where the outward appearance is fair, nor without the strongest proof.
Love “takes no joy in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth.”
See a man who exults at his neighbor’s fall, or cries out, “I told you so”; and I tell you, that man is far indeed from being perfect in love.
It “bears all things”—all provocations and injuries—without revenge.
It “believes all things”; instead of being hard to convince of what is in favor of others, it is always ready to believe good wherever there is the least evidence of it.
It “hopes all things,” even where there is reason to suspect evil, as long as there is room for hope, by putting the best construction on the matter that it will bear.
Where you see an individual who does not have this spirit, rest assured, he is by no means perfect in love.
Indeed, he has no love at all.
I might pursue this line of thought further, but I do not have time.
“Love works no ill to its neighbor.”
Mark that: NO ILL!
Perfect love never overreaches, nor defrauds, nor oppresses, nor does any ill to a neighbor.
Would a man under the influence of perfect love sell his neighbor rum?
Never. Would a man who loved God perfectly, with all his heart, hold his neighbor as a slave?

“Love works no ill to its neighbor”; slavery denies him the wages he has earned, and perhaps sells him and tears him away from his family, deprives him of the Bible, and endeavors as far as possible to make him a brute.
There cannot be greater falsehood and hypocrisy than for a man who will do that to pretend that he loves God.
Now that light is shed on this subject, and the attention of men turned to it.
Will a man hate his own flesh?
How can he who hates or injures his neighbor love God?
I intended to remark on one other effect of perfect love.
It uniformly shows itself in great efforts for the sanctification of the church and the salvation of souls.
Where a person is negligent or deficient in either of these, he is by no means perfect in love, whatever his pretensions may be.

blocks.x: Remarks.

s: I. You see why what the apostle James says is true: “If any man among you seems to be religious, and does not bridle his tongue, but deceives his own heart, this man’s religion is vain.”

The man who professes to be religious, and yet allows himself to speak against his neighbor with an unbridled tongue, to injure his neighbor, deceives himself if he thinks he loves his neighbor as himself. Strange love!
II. There may be much light in the mind concerning religion, without love.
You often see individuals who understand a great deal about religion intellectually, and can set it out before others, while it is plain that they are not moved by the spirit of love.
They do not have the law of kindness on their lips.
III. Those individuals who have much religious knowledge and zeal without love are most unlovely and dangerous persons.
They are always censorious, proud, headstrong, high-minded.
They may make a strong impression, but they do not produce true religion.
They are zealous toward you, but not rightly.
IV. The direction of a man’s zeal will determine the character of his religion.
It will show whether the light in his mind is accompanied by love.
If it is, his zeal will not be sectarian in character.
Show me a man full of jealousy toward all who do not belong to his sect or party, and there is a man far indeed from perfect love.
True love is never condemning or harsh.
If it has occasion to speak of the faults of others, it does so in kindness and with sorrow.
Perfect love cannot speak in a rough or abusive manner, either to others or of them.
It will not lay great stress on the mere incidentals of religion, nor be a stickler for particular measures or forms.
Many will contend fiercely either for or against certain things, such as for or against new measures; but if they were full of love, they would not do it.
The zeal that is governed by perfect love will not spend itself in contending for or against any forms in religion, nor attack minor errors and evils.
Love leads us to lay stress on the fundamentals of religion.
It clings to warm-hearted Christians, no matter what denomination they may belong to, and loves them, and delights to associate with them.
This zeal is never quarrelsome, or full of controversy.
Find a man who loves to attend church assemblies and enters into all the wranglings of the day, and that man is not full of love.
To a mind filled with holy love, it is exceedingly painful to go to such meetings and see ministers dividing into parties, and maneuvering, and caucusing, and quibbling, and striving for the mastery.
Find an individual who loves controversy in the newspapers; he is not full of love.
If he were, he would rather be abused, and reviled, and slandered, either in person or by the papers, than turn aside to defend himself or to reply.
He would never return abuse for abuse, but on the contrary, blessing.
And as much as possible, he would live peaceably with all men.
V. How much of what is called religion has no love!
How much of what passes for works of religion is compelled by outward causes and influences, and not by the inward power of love!

It ought to be better understood than it is that unless love is the mainspring, no matter what the outward action may be—whether praying, praising, giving, or anything else—there is no religion in it. How much excitement that passes for religion has no love!
How much zeal has no religion in it!
See that man, always full of bitter zeal, who, when reproved for it, runs to the example of Paul when he said, “You child of the devil.”
If he were under the influence of perfect love, he would see that his circumstances are so different as not to justify the exercise of such a spirit.
VI. Those religious excitements which do not consist in the spirit of love are not revivals of religion.
Perhaps the church may be greatly excited, and bustle about with a great show of zeal and boisterous noise, but with no tenderness of spirit.
Perhaps those who go about may show a spirit of insolence and rudeness, and pick a quarrel with every family they visit.
I once knew a young man who acknowledged that he aimed at making people angry, and the reason he gave was that it often brought them under conviction, and so resulted in conversion.
And so it might, if he were to go in and utter horrid blasphemies in their presence until they were frightened into considering their own character.
But who would defend such conduct on the ground that this was now and then the result?
And if this is the character of the excitement, it may be a revival of wrath, and malice, and all uncharitableness, but it is not a revival of religion.
I do not mean that when some or many are “filled with wrath,” it is certain evidence that there is no revival of religion.
I mean that when the excitement has this prevailing character, it is not a true revival of religion.
Some among them may have the spirit of love, but certainly those who are filled with a bitter, quarrelsome zeal are not truly religious.
Religion may be revived in some individuals, but in the main, in such cases, it is a revival of irreligion.
VII. When persons profess to be converted, if love is not the ruling feature in their character, they are not truly converted.
However well they may appear in other respects, no matter how clear their views or how deep their feelings, if they do not have the spirit of love to God and love to man, they are deceived.
Let no such converts be trusted.
VIII. See what the world will be when mankind are universally moved by a spirit of love.
We learn that the time will come when there shall be nothing to hurt or destroy, and when the Spirit of love will universally prevail.
What a change in society!
What a change in all the methods of doing business, and in all the dealings of mankind, when each shall love his neighbor as himself, and seek the good of others as his own!
Could one of the saints who live now revisit the earth in that day, he would not know the world in which he had lived; everything will be so altered.
“Is it possible,” he would exclaim, “that this is the earth—the same earth that used to be so full of wrangling, and oppression, and fraud?”
IX. The thing on which the Lord Jesus Christ is bent is to bring all mankind under the influence of love.
Is it not a worthy object?
He came to destroy the works of the devil.
And this is the way to accomplish it.
Suppose the world were full of such men as Jesus Christ was in His human nature.
Compare it with what it is now.
Would not such a change be worthy of the Son of God?
What a glorious end—to fill the earth with love!
X. It is easy to see what makes heaven.
It is love—perfect love.
And it is easy to see what makes heaven begun on earth in those who are full of love.

How sweet their temper, what delightful companions, how blessed to live near them and to associate with them—so full of candor, so kind, so gentle, so careful to avoid offense, so divinely amiable in all things!
And can this be attained by men?
Can we love God, here in this world, with all the heart, and soul, and strength, and mind?
Is it our privilege and our duty to have the Spirit of Christ, and shall we display the spirit of the devil?

Beloved, let our hearts be set on perfect love, and let us give God no rest until we feel our hearts full of love, and until all our thoughts and all our lives are full of love to God and love to man.
Oh, when will the church come up to this ground?
Only let the church be full of love, and she will be fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and as formidable to all wickedness, in high places and low, as an army with banners.
“Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that you may be healed.” — James 5:16
In the present discourse the following points demand our attention.
I. What is intended by the injunction, “Confess your faults one to another”?
II. What is implied in complying with it?
III. The reasons for this injunction.
IV. What is intended by the injunction, “Pray one for another”?

blocks.x: I. What is meant by the injunction, “Confess your faults one to another”?

s: 1. There is no reason to suppose that this text gives any support to the Roman Catholic doctrine of confession to priests.
You understand the doctrine so long prevalent in that communion under the name of “auricular confession,” so called because it was made privately into the ear of the priest.
This doctrine holds that all are bound to make auricular confession of every act and of every thought about which their conscience is at all troubled.
Consequently the system makes the priest the repository of all the sins of the church—of all the most private sins of all its members, male or female, which must be confessed on pain of damnation.
Everyone who is acquainted with the results of this system knows that they have naturally been pernicious to the purity and morals of both priest and people.
It is most evident that the apostle did not have such a system in view and could never approve it.
Confessing faults one to another is not the same thing as confessing all faults to the priest alone.

2. Although there is nothing in the text that specifically defines the sins in view, yet we are doubtless to understand the apostle here to refer primarily to faults committed against others, and to command the confession of faults to those whom we have injured.
The doctrine of confession in this form is abundantly taught and implied in Scripture, and is therefore, we may suppose, the particular thing intended here.
The principle involved in this may, however, extend somewhat further, namely, (1) to the confession or disclosure of our besetting sins and of our particular temptations and weaknesses.

It is plain that by making our trusted Christian friends aware of these temptations and besetting weaknesses of ours, we may enlist their sympathy and prayers on our behalf, and so secure valuable help in resisting and overcoming these temptations.

(2) The principle of the text may also include those sins which, though not properly committed against particular individuals, are nevertheless naturally committed in the presence of others, and therefore become a scandal to religion and a stumbling block to our associates.

For example, irritability, which so often causes others to stumble and becomes a besetting sin; censoriousness—the practice of speaking harshly of others, which is often a painful grievance not only to those against whom we speak evil, but to every benevolent mind that hears us.
These and other sins of this kind, it is plain, should be confessed.

In saying these things, you will notice, I do not say that men are bound to reveal everything they know—all the sins of which they think themselves guilty—even those known to no one but themselves and God.
It does not appear that the Bible makes the duty of confession to men this universal.

blocks.x: II. What is implied in obeying this injunction?

s: 1. That we are thoroughly convinced of our sin; that we admit not only the fact but its wickedness, as a sin against God and our neighbor.
It is one thing for a man to confess his fault as a real fault and a sin, and quite another to acknowledge the fact without recognizing its heinous guilt.
Hence our text must imply that we truly understand and sincerely confess the actual guilt of our sin.
2. That we repent of and renounce our sin.
Confession is no better than an insult to God and man if it is not accompanied by repentance and renunciation of the sin confessed.
3. Humility is also implied.

By this is meant that disposition which is glad to take its own place, even though it is a very low place—which does not seek to gloss over, but truly unmasks oneself and naturally seeks the very place that seems to belong to us.
Commonly the great difficulty found in confessing is that men are too proud.
They do not like to place themselves as low in the estimation of others as they ought to be.
Now humility stands directly opposed to this pride, and implies a willingness to come down to its own low place.
A forced and extorted confession is not what the text commands.

When a man confesses under the sting of a conscience like a scorpion, or because, convicted by public disclosures and confounded by appalling revelations, he cannot do otherwise and still maintain any show of Christianity—such confessions, though they may cost a proud man a tremendous struggle, are yet in real value exceedingly cheap.
4. Genuine confession implies readiness to make restitution for the wrong we have done.

Indeed, confession is in one sense an element of restitution—a part of restitution itself; for example, if you have injured your neighbor in property or in reputation, to confess the fact is one step in the process of restitution.
But it is by no means the whole.
If the case involves property, you must make restitution in kind; if it involves personal reputation, you are bound to make restitution as far as you can.
This is really implied in the spirit of this injunction.
No man in his right mind could suppose that, if he had stolen, his confession would be worth a straw without full restitution.
And the same principle should certainly apply in all cases where restitution is possible.
5. It is implied that the confession be full and free, not scanty and constrained.
Let it be made with a free, full, and honest heart, in such a spirit and manner as will satisfy the reasonable expectations of the injured party.
How can we suppose that God will be satisfied with anything less?
Suppose you have wronged a man, and he knows it and feels it.
You come to him and, after a fashion, you confess; but instead of making a full and satisfactory confession, you merely hint at your wrong deeds.
He knows that you are not an honest man, and that you have not even met the demands of your own conscience.
Such a confession can do neither you nor your neighbor any good.
Confession therefore should be poured out freely as water, full and thorough.
6. Legitimate confession implies and involves throwing yourself upon mercy.
When people thoroughly confess their sins to God, they cease to justify themselves before Him and throw themselves entirely upon His mercy.
They rest upon His clemency alone and leave themselves wholly in the hands of God.
In a similar way, when you confess to a man you throw yourself upon his clemency; you confess your wrong and give up every plea of justification.
7. Where people confess their besetting sins, the act implies a sincere desire to be holy, and an honest determination to give up sin and be rid of it forever.
I have often been struck by the different ways in which different individuals hear the announcement of the doctrine of sanctification.
Proclaim to a body of professing Christians that through grace they may in this life be delivered from all sin, and the way they receive it will often speak volumes in revealing their real character.
It serves to show their exact attitude toward sin.

For example, I once preached in Rochester on this subject, and no sooner had the congregation dispersed than one man came to me, saying with great earnestness, “Mr. Finney, that is too good news to be true.”
There was a minister in that audience, however, who did not regard it as good news at all.
He did not seem to treat the doctrine as if he had any desire for it to be true.
Who has not observed this very difference?
Preach the doctrine of a present salvation from sin to a man who is truly panting to be delivered from sin, and he will hail it with intense interest, if not at once with an open-hearted welcome.
He will receive it most readily if he thinks it may be true.
He will long for it to prove true, and his heart will put no obstacles in the way of his candidly investigating its evidence and heartily embracing all that the evidence can be found to support.

But if he does not want it to prove true, he will quibble against it bitterly—will stubbornly reject its evidence, and of course will be likely to reveal himself unconsciously as the enemy of all righteousness.
He will show that he has no interest in being made free from sin at present—no real interest in being free from sin ever.
These revelations of character are far better testimony to one’s real state of mind than can be given in any other way.
No man who in his heart longed to become holy has ever yet quibbled against this doctrine.
Even if he does not believe the doctrine is true, and therefore feels compelled to oppose it, there will be no spirit of quibbling.
When you see men quibble at any doctrine, you may know they do not want it to be true.
It is not congenial to their hearts.

Who does not know that the doctrine of entire sanctification has lately met with a great deal of opposition under a pretense of zeal for the truth and opposition to error, which after all has been nothing more nor less, before God and the whole world, than a mere spirit of quibbling and a most evident opposition to the truth and unwillingness to have that doctrine proved true?
It has been mournful and appalling to notice the display of real opposition to holiness that has shown itself in many quarters within the last few years.
I am sure I do not say this censoriously.

It is what everybody knows to be true who has kept his eyes open to the real displays that have been made through the pulpit and the press, through church organizations, and in many other ways against the doctrine of holiness in this life.

But to return. When Christians reveal their deep sin to their brethren, it is always implied that they are truly panting after holiness—that they abhor these sins they confess, and are ready to do anything, however humiliating, to put to death these horrible sins they so much hate.

blocks.x: III. Reasons for the injunction, “Confess your faults to one another.”

s: With respect to personal injuries inflicted on others, the injunction is founded on justice.
Confession is a necessary element of restitution.
We cannot be just toward our injured brother without it.
Again, it is indispensable to peace with God.
It is by nature impossible for us to have peace with God without confessing known offenses against our neighbor.
Who needs to be told that God can have no fellowship with injustice, and of course none with those who act unjustly!
Does not His eye mark all iniquity? Your injured neighbor might come before the Lord and say, “Lord, he has wronged me, You know it, and now will You hold fellowship with him?”
Confession is just as indispensable to peace of mind as it is to peace with God.
Suppose all the world were at peace with us, and, if it were possible, suppose God were too; still we could not persuade ourselves that we are right.
Conscience will forever reproach us until we confess and do all we possibly can under the circumstances to make restitution for our wrong deeds.
Confession is indispensable to peace with those whom we have injured.

Although the injured man may have no ill will toward us—no spirit inconsistent with the gospel—no inclination to retaliate, yet it is impossible for him to have the spirit of Christian sympathy and harmony with us as long as he knows us to be impenitent and unwilling to confess known wrongs.
This is a difficulty—a barrier between us—which cannot be removed until he is satisfied that I am honest; and this satisfaction he cannot have until I confess my fault.
Confession is indispensable to peace and sympathy with all the just and good.
While it is true that neither God nor the injured party can be at peace with the wrongdoer until he confesses, the same is equally true of all holy beings.
Their minds cannot be in a peaceful and harmonious state toward me while they know that I am guilty of wrongdoing and will not confess.
As long as they know me to be in this state they must regard me as a transgressor, and this must create an everlasting barrier between me and them.
They may have no inclination to retaliate or to injure me; on the contrary, they may be most earnest in prayer for me that God would humble me and break down my pride.
Their attitude toward me may be nothing other than that of true benevolence; yet until I confess they cannot be in Christian sympathy and friendship with me.
The thing is by nature impossible.
The same is true even of the wicked.
They cannot be at peace with me until I confess my wrongs.
It is remarkable that a wicked man condemns wrongdoing just as truly as a good man does, although he may do the very same thing himself.
His moral judgments about right and wrong may be just and truthful despite his own bad character.
Let him have a case in which his own selfishness does not bribe his conscience and blind his understanding, and he will decide that wrong is wrong and ought to be confessed and put away.
You cannot, therefore, have the respect even of wicked men unless you confess your known wrongs.
Even the wickedest men or devils in hell cannot be satisfied that your course is right until you confess.
They might not love you if you were to become holy, but they certainly can never esteem you until you do—never until you confess and abandon all your known wrongdoing.
They can never justify and approve your sins.
Confession of wrong is indispensable to self-respect.
It is by nature impossible for you to respect yourself while you withhold proper confession of your sins.
By the very laws of your moral nature this can never be.
Who does not know this?
If you do not know this, you certainly can know it, and by a very little careful attention to the warnings of your own conscience you certainly can know it.
Surely you can gain nothing by resisting the claims of an enlightened conscience, for if all the universe should leave you alone in your sin, your conscience would not and could not.
Still its voice would ring in your ear, and you could not silence its reproaches.
Have you not sometimes been ashamed of yourself because you were too proud to confess?

This very shame of making confession has filled your soul with bitter agony and the keenest self-reproach, and you have sometimes felt that it is a greater shame and a deeper guilt than the original wrong itself.
Suppose you were to meet the very man whom you have wronged.
The best opportunity is given to make the confession you know is due—but shame and pride seal your lips.
Not a word of confession is whispered.
You go away full of remorse and a sense of guilty shame, for you can scarcely help feeling that the last sin is worse than the first.
As a physician in these circumstances once cried out, “Oh, how full of hell I am!” so you perhaps are sometimes compelled to say.
You know that what you experience in your soul is a foretaste of hell, for you are all too sure that you deserve the deepest, darkest place in the dwellings of the damned.
No one else can have confidence in you or respect for you as long as it is understood that you will not confess known wrongs.
You may labor to restore yourself to their confidence—but you are doomed to labor in vain.
You may think to live it down, and wash out by good deeds the foul stain attached to you because of unconfessed bad deeds, but you will certainly toil to no purpose.
Who can think you an honest man?
The truth is, they know better; for you have given them the best possible evidence that you are supremely proud and selfish.

Put on the air of a saint as much as you like, you cannot make them trust you as an honest Christian man until you confess your sins wherever confession is, in the nature of the case, fitting and required.
Consider, further, that you can never regain the confidence of discerning men until you are willing to go further in confession than you are absolutely compelled to go.
It often happens that men will go as far as they must, but no further.
They show plainly enough that they move along the path of confession only because they are pushed so hard that they cannot help it.
Step by step—one step at a time, just as fast as they must, but no faster—they move along.
I have often stood and watched this strange process with astonishment.
The guilty man finds that one thing has come out too far to be denied any longer; so he confesses that—but nothing more.
“No,” he says, “that is all.”
Soon another feature of the same transaction comes out, blacker than the first.
“Sir, you are guilty of this too!”
“No, I am not.
You cannot prove it.”
“Yes, my friend, it is proved beyond all question.”
“Oh, well then, I confess that; I am very sorry; but that is all.
There is nothing more.”
Well, by the next day some new point is brought up, and the same road is traveled all over again.
Denial, conviction, confession—and then, to save all the rest of his character, he will beg you to accept his solemn word that there is nothing more of the kind to be revealed.
Now such a man often uses up his character faster than he realizes.
He little thinks how cheap his forced confessions become, and how little confidence is placed in his most solemn declarations that he has made a clean sweep in confession.
