It is far better to go to the bottom at the outset.
Yes, go to the bottom—pour it all out—all of it, so thoroughly that neither man nor God can find anything more belonging to that matter.
Do this, and there is hope for you.
Men will say of you, “Now we know he is honest-hearted, and though he has done wrong, yet he lays his heart wide open, and we can trust him again.”
It is not in human nature to resist the appeal that earnest, honest-hearted confession makes to the human heart.
Again, confession of personal wrongs is exceedingly useful to both parties concerned.
It greatly relieves the guilty man, rolling a mountain’s weight off his soul and restoring sweet peace and joy again.
On the other side, it often seems to be necessary for the party wronged.
You will remember a case I cited not long ago, of Dr. Hopkins, whose deep and wholehearted confessions were the means of converting his wicked brother-in-law.
Confessions will often do what nothing else can.
They often serve to show wicked men that Christians are in spirit utterly unlike themselves.
They are aware that they do not confess their faults like this—that they know nothing of such brokenness of spirit.
Hence the confessions of a humble Christian reach their conscience as nothing else can.
I have often known men to scatter conviction like fire through a congregation by a simple confession of their own sins.
I now remember the case of a minister who, by a confession to his people, set in motion a glorious revival.
He had been to Rome during the great revival there, and had become deeply convicted of his great guilt in having cared so little for the salvation of his people.
He returned home and prepared a sermon for his people, but when he entered the pulpit the next Sabbath, he could not preach it.
His heart was full and ready to burst, and he told the people that he could not preach a word.
“Oh,” he said, “I have been among you so many years, and alas! how little I have cared for your souls!
I have tried to please you, and have carried out my regular duties in a manner all too heartless; but ah, my guilt in having so neglected the salvation of your dying souls!”
Well, he had scarcely begun to confess in this way before the deacon wanted to confess, and then other members of the church, and that house became another Bochim.
The Lord was there, and His work moved on with power.
You can readily see the effect of that minister’s confession.
Everyone said, “If our minister has sins to confess, so do we!
If he has reason to confess with such contrition and bitter weeping, how much more reason do we have!”
So his confessions accomplished what no sermon of his ever did.
Again, sincere confessions are highly honorable to the one who makes them.
There is perhaps no other way in which men show more strongly their earnest and sincere approval of the right.

It is surely no small testimony to the integrity of a man’s character if he shows that he approves the right so fully and strongly that he does not shrink for a moment from condemning himself for any known departure from it.
His love of right prevails over his pride of character.
This man’s confessions are a noble testimony to his deep sincerity of heart.
How strange it is that men should be ashamed to confess their sins!
They could not make this great mistake if they did not “put darkness for light and light for darkness.”
Is it not most honorable for a man who has done wrong to make restitution—for a man who has sinned to make a full and free confession?
How strange that men should be afraid to confess!
They might as well be ashamed to show their honesty—ashamed to let the world see that they approve the right more than they value an undeserved reputation—a reputation for being what they are not.
Confessions serve to unburden the mind of the injured man and lead him to exercise forgiveness.
Injuries inflicted, especially by professing Christians, often become great snares and temptations.
Many are overcome by them and fall into a bad state of mind, in which divine truth and grace seem to have no good influence on their hearts.

They know, perhaps, that it is wrong for them to indulge such feelings, but they have been badly abused, they say—and by a professing Christian, too—and they do not find it easy to rid their minds of the impression thus made.
Now in such cases, an honest confession by the offending party is the natural remedy.
It usually does more to remove that dreadful stumbling block than anything, or everything, else.
Christian reader, is any sinner stumbling in this way over any sin of yours?
Take care that you do not ensnare his soul to his ruin.
Take care that the blood of his murdered soul is not found on your skirts!
I have sometimes known one man to provoke another until he had made him angry, and then reproach him for this very anger, instead of reproaching himself for having caused it.
This is cruelly wicked.

The man who has thus provoked another to anger ought to humble himself in the most thorough confession, and say, “I have most meanly tempted you to sin, and then reproached you for yielding to my temptation—when I ought to have reproached myself most.
I am sorry. I deplore and condemn my own wickedness.”

You may perhaps remember a case in which it is said that a man who was opposing Wesley’s views of sanctification, and who wanted to prove that a certain believer in those views was not perfectly sanctified, went and took a washbowl of filthy water and threw it in his face.
Now let us suppose that the injured man took offense and got angry, and seeing this, the offending party exults and says, “Fine sanctification this—to get angry at so slight a provocation!”
But notice how unspeakably mean and wicked is the course of this tempter to sin.
Let him break down and confess his own sin with shame.
Let him say, “I have been the guilty wretch in this matter!”
Let him do this, and repentance would flow freely from both their hearts.
Again, confession tends strongly to secure the prayers of those against whom you have sinned and to whom you confess.
Nothing tends more strongly to awaken at once the spirit of prayer on your behalf.
How naturally they cry out, “O Lord, forgive the man, for he confesses his wrong; forgive all his sins and show him the light of Your face.”
The confession of our besetting sins to others than an injured party, for the purpose of getting help to overcome them, is exceedingly useful.
It usually interests our Christian brethren very much on our behalf.
Who does not know how powerfully the heart is drawn out to pray for those who confess their besetting sins in this way?
Have you not had some experience of this?
IV. What is meant by praying one for another is easily understood in this connection.
It implies that we take a deep interest in the spiritual welfare of those who confess their faults, and use our influence with God to secure their pardon.
It is as if we were to sign a petition for their release from the sentence of a broken law.

Suppose your neighbor has broken the law of the State and, being convicted, is sent to the State prison for life; but he repents most deeply—gives evidence that he is a changed man—and now a petition for his pardon is laid before you for your signature.
Will you join in the prayer?
Will you say, “Does he confess his sin?
If he does, I can pray for his pardon.”
So when men confess their sins to God and to men, you should pray God to forgive them.
God requires you to do it.
V. Obedience to this requirement implies a real spirit of forgiveness—a desire that God should forgive, and an expression of this desire in real prayer to God.
This is too obvious to need illustration.
Where besetting sins are confessed, it is implied that we take an interest in their sanctification and pray earnestly to God for this great result.

blocks.x: Remarks.

s: 1. Wrongs committed against the public should be confessed publicly.
Of this no one can have any doubt.
If confession should be made at all, it should be made to those against whom the sin is committed.
2. Wrongs against individuals may be committed either publicly or privately, and in either case the confession should correspond to the manner and publicity of the offense.

If any man injures another in public estimation by writing a libel against him, or preaching a libel against him, the sin is public, and clearly the confession of it should be as extensive as the offense.
You are bound to make the retraction as broad as the wrong done, if you can.
3. You may see why many people never overcome their besetting sins.
They are never humble and candid enough to confess them and pour out their hearts before their brethren, so as to secure their sympathy and prayers on their own behalf.
They never take advantage of the great moral lever that confession puts under a man’s giant sins to dig them up and roll them out and away forever.
4. You may see the error of supposing that it is enough to confess to God, and that confession to man is useless and not required.
The Catholic doctrine of confession has driven many Protestants to the opposite extreme, so that many churches are opposed to having any confessions at all made before men.
But it does not follow at all that because Catholics have abused the doctrine of confession, it should therefore be cast away altogether.
It does not follow that we are not under obligation to confess to those whom we have injured.
By no means. If this principle were a just one, we should soon lose all our Bibles.
5. I have often known people to labor a long time under a load of sins unknown to others—sins which there might have been no need to confess, but for their great pride.
But God saw that their pride must be humbled, and He could not give peace to their souls until it was.

Now let such a man go to those whose good opinion he values most and confess his sins; let him truly take up his cross in this matter and not spare his proud heart at all—he will find it a most excellent antidote.
I have often seen this done.
A man goes to some person whom he esteems very highly and says, “I am ensnared by my pride—it is dragging me away from God, down to hell, and I am determined it shall be subdued.”
So he pours out his confession of sin.
Now this is seizing the great club to crush the serpent’s head—the head of cursed pride—and it is commonly successful.
People in this situation will often find confession quite indispensable.
6. When in a case of personal fault both parties are to blame, one should never wait for the other to begin the confessions.
Let each hasten to be most hearty and full in his own confession—then a right spirit will prevail, and each will spur the other on to good.
It often happens that one holds back for fear the other will make bad use of his confessions.
No matter if he does.
I mean, comparatively speaking, it is no matter worth a moment’s regard.
It is infinitely more important that you do what is right before God, the world, and the man you have injured, than that you withhold confession to prevent him from abusing it.
Besides this, there is little danger of his doing so.
If he does, the responsibility is his alone.

In a case of this sort I once knew a man who said, “I will confess my wrong, and if my neighbor does not choose to confess his, or chooses to make bad use of what I confess, he must bear the responsibility alone.”

He poured out his confessions like water, found sweet relief and peace of soul, and soon afterward died; that neighbor and every enemy he had mourned over his ashes in bitterness, and confessed that there had lived at least one good man.

I have known the case of a church involved in great difficulty, its members pitted against each other with strong prejudices and party feelings; but eventually the spirit of confession began to prevail; each man felt himself more to blame than his neighbor, and now the only contest was to see who would confess first and most.
The dispute now was not for each to prove that his neighbor was at fault, but that he himself had been the chief sinner and had been the great cause both of his own sins and of his neighbor’s.
Every man was ready to take his hand off his neighbor and lay it on himself.
This was good. If you could have seen those humbled, confessing Christians, you would have said, “It is good to come down and get the spirit of confession.”
In such circumstances mutual confession seems to be the only thing that can save Christian character and save the church.
When men have done wrong they must come down and confess their faults one to another.
To see two brethren meet in the spirit of mutual confession, forgiveness, and prayer is a blessed sight.
God rejoices in it, and every holy angel strikes a fresh note of joy and praise in heaven.
It is one of the loveliest scenes ever known on earth.
Prayer offered in such circumstances is especially effective.

Suppose you had been wronged—the wrongdoer is prosecuted, convicted, and sentenced—but in the course of time he becomes penitent, you are ready to forgive him, and you send up your petition to the Executive for his pardon.
Now who does not know that your name will carry ten times more weight because of your particular relation to that crime?
So it was in the case of Job and his three friends.
They had spoken unkindly of him, and there was good reason for them to ask his forgiveness.
God’s wrath was kindled against them. What did He say?
“Go,” He said, “to My servant Job—My servant Job shall pray for you, for him I will accept.”
They had accused Job of being a hypocrite.
Now let them make up the matter with Job and obtain his intercession with the Lord on their behalf, and they can be forgiven.
He, above all others, is the man to pray for them.
God can hear him.
Have you wronged a brother?
Go, make your confession to him, and beg his prayers on your behalf.
He is the man to pray for you.
God can hear him.
Humble yourself at his feet until he can feel a spirit of faith to pray for you; then you may hope for prayer that will avail before the Lord.
“Oh,” said a dying slaveholder, “how can I die here on my bed and have no prayer offered up for my guilty soul?”
“What shall I do?” said his sympathizing wife. “Shall I send for the minister?”
“No, no,” said the dying man; “send for my slave Tom.
I have heard him pray in my barn many a time—send for him.”
Tom came softly in, tucked his hat under his arm, and walked toward the bed: “What does Master want?”

“I want you, Tom, to pray for your dying master. I have wronged you and robbed you of your liberty these many years; I am sorry—oh, if I could live to reward you—but if you can pray for a poor lost sinner, do pray!”
And who would not rather have the prayers of the man he had enslaved and wronged than the prayers of all other men on earth?
Such a prayer is worth a world of other prayers!
But how can you have it without confession?
"God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, so that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." —John 3:16
The term world as used here does not mean the globe of earth on which we live, but the human race.
The term is often used in this sense.
The world, the whole world—these are terms often used to signify the people who live in the world, the human race as such.
The term perish in this passage does not mean annihilation; it is clearly set in contrast to everlasting life, as its opposite.

Everlasting life, as the term is used here, is not merely everlasting existence—I do not know that the term is ever used in that sense in any other part of the Bible: whether everlasting existence will be a blessing or not will depend on the state in which individuals exist, whether in happiness or misery.
Under some circumstances everlasting existence might be anything but a blessing.

This everlasting life spoken of here is no doubt an everlasting living with God in heaven—an everlasting existence combined with everlasting happiness; this is the eternal life so often spoken of in the Scriptures, and, no doubt, it is what is meant in this place.

Now to perish is the opposite of this; it is not annihilation or a mere ceasing to exist, because to be annihilated would often be no evil to the individual on whom the sentence was inflicted; to a wretched being it would not be an evil at all, but a great favor.
In short, it is very plain that to perish is the very opposite of everlasting life, and means what is expressed by everlasting death, or a state of endless punishment.
In speaking from these words I propose to consider—
I. The Object of This Love.
II. Its Nature.
III. The Reasons Why This Love Resorted to Such a Measure as Giving the Only Begotten Son of God for Men.
IV. The Nature and Necessity of the Faith That Can Secure This Great End—the Salvation of the Soul.
I. The Object of This Love.
The object of this love is the world—not a part of it, but the world.

There is no reason in the nature of things why one part of mankind should be loved more than another part, because, note well, this love was not exercised toward saints as such, and had no regard to the character of the people of the world; rather, it was toward a world of sinners that this love was exercised.
God loved men as a race, as sinners, the enemies of God.

Now there was no reason why part of the race of sinners should be loved, and not all of them; and the same kind of love that could possibly love a part of mankind must, by necessity and from its very nature, love the whole of them—this is the only love, a universal love, that could have been exercised toward man by a good being.
But this leads me to inquire, in the next place, into—

blocks.x: II. The Nature of This Love.

s: And first, I observe that it could not have been a love of approval, or a delight in the character of men, for there was nothing in the character of the human race that could allow God to love them, or take any delight in their character—that is most certain.
It is impossible that God should have loved mankind with an approving love; for that would have made him infinitely more wicked than they were themselves.
What does it imply to love a wicked being?

Why, it implies sympathy with his character: God could not have loved them with an approving love without being infinitely more wicked than they, because for an infinite being to sympathize with wicked natures he must himself be infinitely wicked.
It is certain that this love could not have had any regard to the character of men—they were not loved for their character; it is impossible that it should have been so.

But I remark again, this love could not have been mere emotion, for emotion does not influence the life apart from the will; emotion is not a cause; it will not bring anything into existence—even intense emotion will not; it is a merely involuntary state of mind—something that belongs to the passions; it will often be a motive to action, and may be a stimulus to the will, but mere passion never caused anything; causality is that which produces, and it lives in the will of every moral agent, and is a very different thing from emotion.
Again, it was not fondness for particular persons.
There was no reason in God's nature, and no reason in man, why God should exercise any such fondness.
I remark again that it was not an involuntary love, as is evident from what it did.
It must have been voluntary, because we have here before us the evidence of its effectiveness; and it was an effective love because it was a voluntary love.
Again, it was not an unreasonable state of mind.
There was, to be sure, nothing in the character of man that would allow for an approving love, yet it was not an unreasonable state of mind at all; it was not something forbidden by reason.
We sometimes see affections among men that are wholly unreasonable.
We sometimes see deep affection, in the form of what we call love, existing among people in a way that is totally contrary to reason.
But there was some good reason for this love of God—something that his own understanding and conscience approved.
There was something about men that made it reasonable for God to love them with a certain kind of love.
I remark again that the love God actually did show was the only kind of love that could have been of importance to man.
If the love of God had been mere emotion, or pity, it would have done man no good.
This love, then, must have been a reasonable affection; it must have been a reasonable love.
Now when we look at the nature of this love, if we do so in a simple and reasonable manner, there can be no doubt about what its real nature is.
I observe that it was good will, or benevolence.
This is evident from the fact that it exerted itself for the good of its objects in a most striking and wonderful manner.
It is plain that it was good will, because it produced good action.
Again, it was an unselfish kind of love.
The reason God loved men was not that they deserved for him to do them good—for they deserved only evil at his hands.

Note well, there was a good reason why he should love them, but they had no right to demand his love as a matter of justice, for they had forfeited all claim to his affection or protection; and therefore, of course, justice did not demand that God should do them good.

But let me say once more, the soul of man was so valuable, its happiness would be so infinitely important, and its misery so great an evil, that God, looking at the intrinsic value of their souls, saw good reason for loving them and doing them good—that is, God did the good for the sake of the good itself; he willed good to them for the sake of the intrinsic and infinite value of this good to them, considered in itself, and not because they deserved it at all.

They not only had no claim on him for this love, but there were great reasons for his destroying them; yet, nevertheless, so great was the value of their souls, so much did he pity them in view of their coming and certain destruction, and so greatly did he love their happiness and desire it, that, overcoming all obstacles in the way, he rose above any inclination to punish them or retaliate against them for their wickedness, and sought only to do them good.
There was good reason for this, as I have said—not in view of the actions of mankind, but in consideration of the value of their souls.

I remark once more that this love was a disinterested love; I mean that he did not set before himself any interest of his own merely as the reason why he should do this thing—it was the love of the world—it was a disposition to do them good; it was the love of their good that led him to do it.
He did not propose to benefit them in any such sense as to secure for himself, in any selfish sense, some great good—it was a totally disinterested love.
As a matter of fact he did enjoy it himself, and yet it was a totally disinterested love, and all the more will it glorify him.
Just in proportion as he aimed to secure their interest with singleness of purpose, in just that proportion did he secure his own approval and the admiration and glorification of all holy beings.

By disinterested love I do not mean that he had no interest in it, for he had an infinite interest in what he did; but I mean that his love was wholly unselfish—he sought to do good because of the value of the good itself.
But let me say again: this must have been a love of amazing strength; it could not have been a feeble state of mind; it must have been infinitely intense!
Just think of it!
"For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son!"
What a wonder that was!
Here, on the one hand, was a world of enemies who were at war with him; and on the other stood his beloved Son, his only begotten, his well-beloved Son.

Now just look at this, and conceive of a state of mind that would prefer to give that Son, that only begotten, that well-beloved Son, to die for those rebels who stood with the weapons of rebellion in their hands.

They had revolted against his government, and were deserving of his frown and his wrath, his own conscience clearly affirming that they deserved to be banished from his presence; yet such was his estimate of the value of their souls, and of the dreadful suffering to which they would be subjected if the penalty of the law were inflicted on them, that he gave his Son rather than banish that world of rebels from the glory of his power to die in their guilty state.
No one, unless he ponders these things well, will understand how intensely strong this love must have been to produce such a determination as that.

Let a parent who has an only child conceive, if he can—a child who has never offended him, the very darling of his soul, one whom he loves as much as he loves himself and has reason to love—whether he could give up that child for the good of his enemies.

Let people abuse him, do everything they possibly could to injure him, placing themselves in a position as offensive as possible so as to deserve his indignation and condemnation, and incur his utter rejection and his abhorrence of them forever.
Now conceive of a state of mind that could deliberately make such a choice as God did.

It was not the sacrifice of an innocent person in place of the guilty; it was not the punishment of Christ—consenting that Christ should suffer instead of sinners being punished—no; there was no such idea in the divine mind.
But we shall inquire more fully later on into the reasons why God gave his Son to die for the good of the world.
I am now speaking of the intense nature of this love.

Now think, if you can, with your son on one side and your enemies on the other, what struggles would arise in your mind as you reflected on the fact that these enemies must perish forever or you must give up your son!

You see that he has a willing heart, that he is ready to undertake their deliverance from death—that he is willing to take on all that is implied in being their Savior; but it requires that you consent to it, that you enter into it with your heart, and that you say to him, Go.

Now when we realize what God must have felt under such circumstances, it is easy enough for us to understand the intense nature of the love that could overcome that state of mind which would naturally cling to his Son, and give him up for the good of the world.
Just consider how many things there must have been against this.
God knew what it would cost him, that his Son must pass through trial, through affliction, through persecution, through poverty, through agony.

His Father saw every trial and every suffering that he would have to undergo—he saw him heavy with sorrow and despised—he saw him, too, in the garden, when he sweated, as it were, great drops of blood, so great was his agony—all this was present to the divine mind when he gave up his Son to be the Savior of the world.
The Father saw his Son weary to the point of fainting as he carried his cross up Calvary's hill, so that his barbarous persecutors were compelled to lay the burden on another.
He saw him mocked and pierced when on the cross, and saw him in the agonies of death, and heard his mournful cry, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
What a number of scenes must have clustered around the divine mind to forbid the gift of his Son for the salvation of a guilty world.
Yet so great was his love that he overcame all these obstacles and freely gave him up for us all, so that we might not perish but have everlasting life.
Let this idea, dear hearers, take possession of your minds.

I must not enlarge on this, however, but proceed to say that it must never be forgotten or left out of view that it was the love of enemies, not of friends; for, note well, all the world was in view, and it was as sinners that God gave Christ to die for them—they were a race of sinners.
Note well, it was not for a single Christian, as such, that God gave his Son; it was for sinners as such, for rebels as such; it was in view of the fact that they were sinners that God gave his Son.
Now it is very important that this fact always be kept in mind: that it was not for good but for bad people, not for the righteous but for the wicked, that God gave his Son.
Again, it was a forbearing love.
Some people seem to think that when we speak of the self-denial of God we imply that he is sometimes selfish.
Now let me say, self-denial always implies the very opposite of selfishness in any being; it is consenting to give up some good, or to endure some evil, for the benefit of others.
No individual who is living in selfishness can, of course, exercise self-denial.
Now this was self-denial in God, to consent to deny himself by giving up his Son; it must have been greatly trying to his feelings for him to consent to give up his Son to die for the world.
But I must not enlarge on this.
Let me say again: it was, of course, a universal love.
It was not love for men alone; it extended to other worlds.
And no doubt it was, in great measure, with reference to other worlds that he was led to take the course he did take in forgiving sin in this world.
It was the good of his universal kingdom that led him to take this particular measure.
Again, his love was a holy love; it hated sin.

Since this love was exercised toward sinners, it was very important that something should be done to make the whole universe understand that, although it was the love of sinners as such, it was not connivance at their sin.

Indeed, this was the grand and most essential point, as every man can see: since his love was a love shown to sinners, how he should sufficiently guard against the impression that he connived at their sins; for, note well, he was going to express great love for sinners by devoting himself to doing them good.
Now, mark this: how shall it be known that he was as much opposed to their sin as he had professed to be, and as the universal conscience demanded that he should be?
It is often a delicate thing for human rulers to show love and benevolence to those who are rebels against the government.
It is a very delicate thing for the governments of great and extensive empires to show deep and anxious love for those who are enemies of the law and who defy it.
There is also much danger that the justice of the law will be thrown into the shade, that respect for the law will be lost sight of, and that the sin involved in the rebellion will be forgotten.

Now there was infinite danger of this in the government of God; therefore it was necessary that, while pardoning the sinner, he should as much as possible show his opposition to sin, and so make it plain to the world that he did not connive at their sin.
But again, this love was just as truly as it was merciful; that is, it was just to the universe.
There were other interests in his government besides the interest of sinners.
There were reasons why he should not endanger his authority and lower respect for his law.
Now it is easy to see that justice to the universe demanded that he be careful how he expressed the great and infinite love he had in his heart toward sinners.
This leads me to consider—
III. The Reasons for This Wonderful Measure of the Divine Government.

His love, note well, sought to accomplish the world's salvation—he sought to save those who deserved to die, and we are told that he resorted to this measure of giving his only begotten Son for sinners—a wonderful measure indeed!
Now it is plain that the reason for this must have been anything but ill will on the part of God.
Again, it was anything but anger at them that led him to do it.

To be sure, from one point of view, he had a holy indignation at their sins; but it was not this anger that led him to give his Son—he gave him in spite of this just and holy indignation at their sins.
It was not God's anger, then, but a merciful disposition that led God to require Christ to die for sinners.

God was disposed to be merciful; this was the secret of the whole matter; this was the grand foundation of the whole arrangement: the very reason God undertook their salvation was that he loved them, and was disposed to show them favor.
It was not, then, I say, the lack of a merciful disposition; it was not hatred, but love of sinners—the one great reason that led God to show mercy to men.
There was one great reason in the divine mind, the fundamental reason: his love for sinners.

Now mark this: it is said that God resorted to this measure of giving his Son to secure the good of the world—for several reasons, which I will name, he did not retaliate against them for all their opposition to him.
Now observe, there must have been some very weighty reasons, and some reasons that needed to be overcome, but which could not be overcome by any measure other than the one that was actually adopted.
We ought always to understand that God acts rationally, and for wise and good reasons.
Let no one, therefore, suppose that he resorted to any unnecessary measure of severity.
No one can rationally suppose that God resorted to any means that could have been avoided in the nature of the case.
Now he had set his heart on the means—wise means, and means that were demanded by the circumstances and the occasion.
Who can believe that any other means were resorted to?
But let us look at the reasons for the particular measure that was taken.
It is of very great importance to understand them.

We have seen that God had a good reason for the measure he adopted—a sufficient reason, and a reason that could not have been set aside or overcome; but let us now find out, if we can, what these reasons were.
Whatever they were, they must have been approved by the law of benevolence, or they could not have been virtue.
If the measure had not been one approved by the eternal laws of God's own reason, he never could have resorted to it.

But the fact is, it is simple enough, and it does not require any great learning to understand it: it only needs to be looked at, and everyone can see at once that such circumstances called for such a measure.

Look at the subject—mankind had resisted the government of God, and had denied the justice of his law, to which even the angels conform, and which is absolutely necessary to secure the well-being of the universe and their own salvation.
Now if God had seemed to connive at man's disobedience of his law, which was the law of the entire universe, all other beings might have denied the justice of the law and disobeyed it also.
Observe, therefore, that the whole universe, all the inhabitants of heaven, had a strong interest in maintaining this law.
Now mark this! This law had been disobeyed; a public lie had been told and persisted in; the justice of the law had been denied in a most deliberate manner.
Now what was to be done?
It is evident that something must be done that could not be construed as connivance at this rebellion.
Now observe the relations between man and God.
God's law had been trampled underfoot, and the universe had its eye on God to see what he would do—the well-being of the whole depended on it.
His relation to the universe required of him either to execute the law or to make a demonstration on his own part, from his own heart—for it was his estimation of the law that the universe needed.
It was for him to act, and everything depended on the course he took.

It is easy to see that the honor of the law might be fully upheld by God himself, if he should show before the whole universe his approval of the law and of the public good—and such a demonstration as this would serve the same end as the execution of the law on the offenders.

If God would take upon himself human nature, and in this nature of both God and man would stand right out before the whole universe and yield obedience to its precepts, this would be as high an evidence of his regard for the law as he could possibly give in any way whatever.
By taking upon himself the nature of the violators of the law, and in that nature obeying the precept and suffering the penalty, the demonstration would be complete and the law perfectly honored.

Now suppose that Christ, his eternal Son, should in this way stand forth as the representative of the race of rebels, having no sin in himself, and yet standing in such a position as if the sin of the whole race were summed up in him and the whole rebellion centered in him; it is easy to see that God could pardon the sinners and yet honor the law.

Mark this! He stands as the representative of the world, as the representative of sin, and it is easy to see that this arrangement was a great deal more impressive than the execution of the law on the rebels themselves would have been.
The lawgiver himself stands forth as an illustration of the beauty of his own law, and in vindication of its honor.
But I must not enlarge on this.

I have only to say under this head that it is perfectly easy to see the bearing of this measure on the universe itself: how perfectly it met the urgent need of the government, and made it quite safe for God to pardon the guilty.
I shall now, in the next place, make a few remarks on—
IV. The Nature of Faith.
Now observe the motive that caused God to do this thing.

I have sometimes heard people speak of the atonement of Christ, and of God's motive, in such a manner as to show that if they believed God had any such motive as they ascribed to him, it was quite impossible for them to have any respect for him.

They speak of the atonement as not coming from a merciful disposition in God, but as the exacting of a debt; that God required a certain amount of payment for every sinner before he would forgive; that it was not the result of a merciful disposition.
Now I say that if anyone believes this, he cannot even have respect for the character of God.
Now we are taught that God gave his Son to die for men as sinners, and out of love for them, and that they receive the blessing as the result of exercising faith in Christ.
It is that which gives it all its power.
Only let a sinner understand that God loves him as a sinner, and if there is anything that can break his heart, that will.
I do not mean to say that a knowledge of this fact will invariably do it; but I do say that if this does not, nothing will.
In short, the declaration of love to sinners must be realized and believed by them in order for them to be saved.
A few remarks must close what I have to say.
First, many people overlook the nature of this love because they cannot conceive how God can love sinners.
I know this from my own experience, for I stumbled at this point for a long time.
I had not experienced benevolent love at all.
I had exercised love: I knew what the term meant in some of its senses.

I knew what it was to take delight in those whose characters I admired; and I knew what the love of fondness meant as it exists among selfish beings; but, note well, this was the only kind of love I had exercised, and therefore I could not understand how God could love a wicked man: it seemed to me impossible that God should love a sinner.
I said to myself, If God can love a sinner, he must himself be a sinner; and do you think that God can be a sinner?
Now you see, I judged God by my selfish love.
The love that I exercised implied some fellowship and sympathy with the one loved.
At last I was enabled to understand that God could love men without exercising a selfish love.
A great many people speak very loosely on this subject; they do not understand the nature of God's love for sinners—the selfish mind cannot.
When a sinner first becomes convicted of sin, he thinks it is perfectly impossible for God to love him, and is ready to exclaim, He cannot love me any more than he can love the devil.
And in part that is true.
He cannot love the sinner with an approving and sympathizing love any more than he can the devil—not a bit more.
But there is another view of this subject, which it is very important for you to take, sinner; there is a kind of love to which you are a stranger—the love of your enemies.
Oh, you say, what reason have I to love them?
Why, you have the same reason to love them that God has—exactly!
God does not love with an approving love, which implies sympathy with their characters; but do not be mistaken, sinner, he can love you with a love of which you have no conception.

Now the kind of love that God will exercise is just the kind that you ought to exercise toward your enemies; and in order to receive this love you must rise entirely above your selfishness, and give yourselves up with hearty good will to seek their good.
Now the fact is that, because you have never exercised this love, you cannot understand its nature.
But God can rise above—ah, he never was in the selfish mire that your soul is in.

He is not filled with the spirit of retaliation that you feel—and therefore, although he sees and knows all the guilt of the sinner, he can still look upon him with compassion, and devote himself with all his heart to saving him.
But let me say once more: the fact is, sinners mistake the nature of God's love, and so they try to make themselves happy.

They always suppose that they must do something to deserve his love; you ask them to come to Christ, and they say, I must do more; I must become better; I must pray; I must do this thing or the other thing to deserve his love.
They have, you see, the idea of approving love; they must deserve it before they have it—they want to feel that they deserve it.
The sinner will never believe that God loves him as a sinner.
But let me tell you, sinner, that this is all wrong; you can never deserve God's love in the sense in which you hope to possess it—and if you seek to deserve it in that way, you will never be saved.
But remember, it was as a sinner that Christ died for you!
It was as a rebel that God gave his Son to die for you!
Just as you are in your sins, God loves you, and for you, just in that state, he gave his Son to die for you.
This is what you must believe.
You will find it difficult to believe, but it is absolutely necessary that you do so.
Let me urge you to let this idea take full possession of your minds, and say to yourself, What need is there, then, to try to make myself deserving, if God loves me now just as I am?

It was as I am that Christ died for me; it was as a sinner that God loved me, and loves me still; as a sinner, then, I will go to Jesus, as I am, as a humble penitent—a seeking, but not a deserving, sinner.
Will you come? Will you come now?
Will you believe now? Or will you make God a liar?
“Repent, therefore, of this your wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you.
For I perceive that you are in the gall of bitterness, and in the bonds of iniquity.” Acts 8:22–23
These words were addressed to Simon Magus.
A revival of religion was in progress in Samaria under the labors of Peter and Philip; many were converted to God, and among them Simon Magus also professed conversion.
He had been a great man in that place and had deceived many by his magic arts.

Seeing the greater wonders worked by these Christian apostles, he was struck with surprise, and his ambitious spirit seized on the idea of increasing his own power over men by obtaining this new secret.
So he offers the apostles money to buy this new power.
Peter saw his heart at once and nobly replies: “Your money perish with you; you have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right in the sight of God.”
He then gives him directions as in our text: “Repent, therefore, of this your wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you.”
Following the order of thought in the text, I will
I. NOTE THE PRINCIPLE DEVELOPED HERE, IN THE LIGHT OF WHICH PETER SAW THAT THIS MAN WAS STILL IN HIS SINS;
II. SHOW WHAT REPENTANCE IS;
III. WHAT IS IMPLIED IN REPENTANCE;
IV. SHOW WHY SINNERS ARE EXHORTED FIRST TO REPENT, AND THEN TO PRAY FOR PARDON;
V. DWELL ON THE IMPORTANCE OF FOLLOWING THIS EXAMPLE IN ALL OUR DEALINGS WITH MEN.
I. Peter did not claim to learn Simon Magus’ character by inspiration.
He had no such omniscience.
He doubtless had inspiration, but inspiration taught general truth, not individual character.
Peter saw his heart to be selfish, and not at all in harmony with the spirit of the gospel.
Simon still had his old spirit, and wanted power to give the Holy Spirit to whomever he pleased, for the same reason that he had previously sought and valued his magic powers.
That is why he offered money, as if the apostles were as sordid as himself.
Peter saw that he was selfish and therefore blind, far indeed from understanding the subject of Christianity.

blocks.x: II. Therefore Peter urged him to repent. What is repentance?

s: Repentance should always be distinguished from conviction of sin.
The latter is an involuntary state of mind, and of course has no virtue in it.
There may be as much of it as there is in hell itself, and yet no virtue.
There is awful conviction in hell, but no genuine repentance.
Neither does repentance consist merely in sorrow.
Indeed, this is properly and strictly no part of it, for sorrow does not belong to the thinking faculty of the mind—much less does it belong to the will and to the faculty of voluntary action.
Nor again is repentance the same thing as remorse.
Remorse, though it amounts to the keenest and most galling self-condemnation, does not necessarily imply repentance.
There may be no change of mind in it whatever.
Repentance is simply and precisely a change of mind.
The original term means a thinking again—a turning of the mind—as when someone finds himself going wrong and turns around to pursue the opposite course.
The term, when applied to evangelical repentance, means not merely a turning of the mind, but a change of the entire purposes of action, a change in the entire attitude of the will.

Repentance, therefore, is not remorse, is not sorrow, is not anything of this kind; but it is the mind turning away from selfish attitudes to benevolent ones—from being selfish to being truly benevolent.

blocks.x: III. What is implied in repentance?

s: 1. Conviction of sin as a wrong committed against God.
Without this there can be no rational repentance.
2. That the sinner becomes truly honest with God.
He must honestly admit the truths affirmed by his reason and pressed on his soul by his conscience.
Especially must he recognize God’s rights—that he himself is God’s property and truly belongs to God.
3. That he becomes just and fair toward men—truly an honest man.
Selfishness is the greatest dishonesty in the world.
No man who is selfish is fundamentally honest, unless a man can be honest while practically denying everybody’s rights but his own.
No; selfishness is the perfection of dishonesty.
It is absurd for a wicked man to pretend to be honest.
He has not a particle of genuine honesty, any more than Satan has!
What is honesty? Respecting all other men’s rights, and especially God’s rights, according to their true value.
But the sinner sets himself up as an honest man while he utterly denies God’s rights.
How false their claims are!

They respect their neighbor’s rights only for their own interests—only because in some way they expect to reap good for themselves from the respect they hypocritically show to their neighbor’s interests.
The fact is, men are completely deceived if they think themselves honest toward men while they are not truly honest toward God.
The heart of honesty is not in them.
If they do not love their neighbor as themselves, they are not honest.
No man has a right to say in practice that his rights and interests are greater than his neighbor’s.
The practical assumption of this is both false and dishonest.
4. No man is penitent who is not an honest man in the sense that he renders to God what is God’s and to man what is man’s.
He must begin by restoring to God his stolen self.
God has created him, has kept him alive, and has redeemed him—this threefold claim God has on him; and yet he sets himself up in opposition against God and has no sympathy with God whatever.
No man, therefore, is honest until he repents toward God.
The first step is to give himself back to God, and with himself whatever remains of his time, his talents, his property, and his influence.
It is always implied in true repentance that you make full restoration of everything you have not so squandered that you feel it is beyond your power to restore it.
5. Repentance implies confession of sin to God and to all those whom you have injured.
Let no man think himself truly penitent until he has made confession in all things where it is due.
Some sins are known only to God, and some are committed only against God.
These should be confessed to God.
In some exceptional cases, God holds men to the duty of confessing secret sins.
This, however, is the exception and not the rule.
I cannot enter now into the distinctions that should be made on this subject.
But obviously, where restitution cannot be made without confession—as, for example, where someone’s character has been injured—there you persist in the wrong unless you confess.
You have deceived many about your neighbor, to his hurt, and this wrong which you have done him you must undo, or you cannot suppose yourself to be truly penitent.
6. But besides confession, restitution is always implied in repentance.
Each man should make it to the extent of his power.
This is always implied, because the penitent man is also benevolent.
He loves his neighbor as himself, and therefore, like Zacchaeus, he hastens to restore, and thinks it no hardship even to restore fourfold.
7. Repentance implies the complete abandonment of all courses of life and of business that are inconsistent with Christian character.
Do you think that a man truly benevolent in spirit could pursue a business fitted to ruin men instead of saving them?
No indeed! Shall a man who loves the well-being of others as he does his own devote himself to trafficking in human flesh?
No sooner than he would sell his own flesh and blood—his own person into bondage, or the bodies and souls of his own wife and children!
8. Repentance also implies an abandonment not only of all selfish branches of business, but of all selfish ways of conducting business, even business that is right in itself.
Selfish men often pursue a good business in a bad way—on most selfish principles and policies.
This also repentance rules out, because repentance is a change of the heart and life from selfishness to real benevolence.
It implies an abandonment of all selfishness.
9. Repentance implies a universal reformation of life—a reformation extending to all forms of sin.
Penitent men turn from all sin as sin—because they regard it as sin, and therefore can have no sympathy with it.
Therefore they at once abandon all known sin.
And since to them nothing can be sin except what is known to be such, the forsaking of all known sin is really the forsaking of all sin.
No man is truly penitent who allows himself to continue in some chosen sin, and who picks and chooses his indulgences.
This is not repentance at all.
When I speak of abandoning sin, I do not mean that the penitent man never relapses into it even for a moment; but I mean that he sets himself against it with real honesty and earnestness.
10. Finally, true repentance implies confidence in God and in Jesus Christ.
If a man truly repents of sin, he will of course believe in Jesus Christ.

blocks.x: IV. What is implied in the successive order of duties as Peter commanded them—repentance before prayer for pardon?

s: 1. He assumed that Simon Magus was totally depraved—totally alienated from God, and therefore unwilling to give up his sins.
So he could not urge him to pray for pardon while he was still in his sins.
Peter knew very well that Simon would leap at the idea of being forgiven before he repented; but he meant to warn him in the strongest way against such a delusion.
He knew that his sin consisted in clinging to his selfishness, and therefore told him first to give up his sins and then to ask forgiveness.
Peter assumed that his unwillingness to give up his selfishness was his great sin, to be repented of and put away first of all.
2. He assumed that God could not forgive him until he put away his sin.
Peter knew Simon’s great difficulty—knew that he held on to his course as an ambitious and selfish man; and therefore assured him that mercy could come to him only after full repentance.
3. Peter did not regard Simon as having any right to ask or wish for pardon until he had repented.
You will notice that Peter saw Simon as impenitent and selfish.
So he assumed that he had no right to ask or expect forgiveness while in this state of mind.
He did not tell him to pray for repentance, because he knew he was unwilling to repent, and therefore such a prayer would only be mocking God.
Yet many direct the sinner to pray for repentance!
Ah, do you want the sinner to mock God?
Peter did not direct Simon to pray for repentance, for he knew that this would only be mocking God until Simon himself was willing to repent; and he could not invite him to insult Jehovah.
4. It is also assumed that he was fully able to repent.

Men sometimes teach sinners to pray that God would make them able to repent, and many even imply that the sinner is trying as hard as he can to repent, and therefore needs only to cry to God to help him repent—the only difficulty in his case being that God does not give him enough strength!
“Trying to repent” always implies two things—a willingness to repent, and a lack of power to do it.
Trying is making an effort to accomplish what the mind is set on, and, if unsuccessful, implies that the failure results from lack of power.
Now Peter understood this whole subject.
Peter knew that this man had free will enough and ability enough to repent if he would.
Therefore he directs him first to repent, and then to ask pardon.
Asking forgiveness before repenting would only blaspheme God, and Peter could not advise him to do that.
5. Peter implies that he had conviction enough, and therefore need not wait for more.
So he did not tell him to wait for it, but to repent at once.
This of course assumed that he had conviction enough.
Many set sinners to praying for conviction just as if they needed more and desired to have it, neither of which is usually true.
6. Peter assumed that the sinner is without excuse, whether for his sin or for his remaining impenitent.
He insisted on repentance as the present duty of that man, which of course implies that in God’s judgment it is the duty of every sinner to repent.
Now it must be of the very first importance for us to know how God judges in this matter.
It is a remarkable fact that Peter and all the other inspired teachers agree in representing God as requiring sinners to repent at once.

blocks.x: V. It is of the utmost importance to follow this inspired example. For,

s: 1. This direction to repent before asking forgiveness, and this alone, is consistent with the facts of the case.
For what are the facts?
Simply these. The sinner is a free-acting, voluntary agent.
In this capacity he sets himself selfishly against the demands of God’s law of love.
Now what shall God require him to do?
Change his course, to be sure—in other words, repent.
Nothing can be plainer than that a voluntary agent who is voluntarily doing wrong should turn around and voluntarily do right.
This, and this alone, is consistent with the facts and with the right of the case.
But suppose you undertake to give direction to a sinner who is still selfish, that is, devoted to pleasing himself.
First of all you set him to praying.
Praying for what? That God would give him the desire of his heart?
Of course, if he prays without first changing the purpose of his heart, he will pray for what he desires—that is, he will pray that God would grant him the selfish desires of his heart.
His prayer would be: O Lord, let me have heaven without holiness; Lord, pardon my sins, and yet let me go on living in sin, for I have no heart to repent!
Now can such mocking of God be of any use?
Would you think it likely that the Bible would give such directions to awakened sinners?

If men are truly willing to repent and forsake all sin, God asks no more of them, for the willing is essentially the doing; but there can be no greater mistake in this world than to assume that sinners are willing to repent and want to repent before they actually do it.

2. The usual order in which inquirers are set to work is the reverse of the order commanded in the Bible, as if the sinner were ready and God not ready, and therefore the sinner needs to use means to make God ready and to urge Him forward to do His duty.
3. To set the sinner to praying for repentance is to assume that he is willing to repent but cannot, and therefore needs God’s power to help him.
The truth is, no man can will to renounce sin without doing so; for to will it is to do it.
4. To direct sinners otherwise than God does in the Bible is to deceive them.
Thousands have been deceived in this way to the ruin of their souls forever.

If you set them to pray for pardon before they repent, you leave them under the delusion that they are doing something they ought to do—that they are doing their duty—whereas they are not doing their duty until they repent!
What a horrible doctrine this is!
Teach an impenitent sinner, still holding on to his sins, to pray for pardon!
This would ruin a world of sinners.
It would leave them all deceived and deluded in their sins and under God’s wrath forever!
5. To tell the sinner to pray for the Holy Spirit is only the same thing in a slightly different form.
Nothing can be more deceptive than to tell the sinner to pray for the Holy Spirit while you know he is only resisting the Holy Spirit, and while you allow him to go on, still resisting.
“You always resist the Holy Spirit,” says the word of God through one of its most faithful and truthful preachers.
What does the Holy Spirit do?
He takes truth and reveals it to the sinner in impressive aspects.
This is His office-work with respect to the sinner.
As soon as the sinner yields to the truth as presented and enforced by the Holy Spirit, he is converted.
Until he repents, he only resists the Spirit.
What good does it do, then, to direct him to pray for the Spirit, as long as he is resisting the Spirit?
What can his prayer be while he pursues this course, except mocking God?
What he should do is not to pray for the Holy Spirit, but to yield to His influence as it is already exerted on his mind.
The first thing and the only right thing for the awakened sinner to do with reference to the Spirit is to yield his heart to the demands of God’s revealed truth.
Let him do this, and he would be converted in a moment.
He should be told that he does not feel his need of the Spirit, and therefore cannot pray intelligently for the Spirit’s greater influence on his mind.
He should also be told that the only honest thing he can do in the first place is to stop resisting the Spirit.

Peter did not say to Simon, “Pray for the Holy Spirit to strive with you, or to repent for you, or to make you repent, or even to help you repent”; but simply, “Repent yourself—repent first of all, and then ask forgiveness.”
6. To direct a sinner who is still in his sins to pray instead of repenting is to leave him under the impression that after he has prayed he has done his duty.
You tell him to pray; he prays, and then says, “Now I have done my duty, so why am I not converted?”
But if you tell him, as Peter did, first to repent and then to pray—if he follows your direction, he is converted, and then his prayer can be acceptable to God.
The opposite course—that is, the reverse order, which puts prayer before repentance—virtually casts the blame for continued impenitence upon God.

If you direct the sinner to pray first instead of repenting first, you virtually imply that the difficulty in the sinner’s way is one that God must remove—that the reason he has not repented lies in God, not in himself.
If the sinner follows your direction, he prays before he repents, and then, having prayed, he says, “Why am I not converted and saved?”
“I have prayed; God does not convert me; let the blame be on God and not on me!” How horrible the influence of this course must be on the sinner’s mind!
7. No inspired writer warrants any course other than this one in the text.
Search the Scriptures from beginning to end; you find no directions to sinners different from this.
You might well wonder in amazement if you did, for to bid the sinner go and pray first before repenting overlooks the very nature of repentance and of a sinning state of mind.
8. Every doctrine of Scripture is consistent with the course of directions given in the text, and with no other course.
Every doctrine of Scripture shuts the sinner up to the doing of present duty.
The whole Bible urges him to do present duty, and if he is in unrepented sin, it tells him that his first duty is to repent.

Men have struck out on a strange path of their own, directing sinners to do something other than repent; but the Bible holds steadfastly to the only consistent course—urging on every sinner, always, that first of all he should repent.
John came crying in the wilderness of Judea, “Repent!” and Jesus Christ followed him preaching the same thing and nothing different from this: “Repent,” He says, “for the gospel kingdom is at hand.”
So every prophet and every apostle, each in his place, cried aloud, “Repent, REPENT,” as if there were nothing else they dared to say until this first duty is done.
This is the only rational course—the only course that is based on Scripture, on reason, and on the true science of the mind.
Every sinner knows that he is a sinner.
You no more need the Holy Spirit to make you see yourself as a sinner than to make you see that you exist.
This shows why the Bible always faces the sinner down with the assumption: You are a sinner, and the fact needs no proof.
Every sinner knows it.
9. Sinners are often very willing to pray, but not to repent.
Only let him off from the heart-work of repenting, and he will gladly do many other things.
A young man once said to me, “I would travel to any part of the world if I might be saved by it.”
“Yes,” I said, “but one thing you will not do: give up your self-righteousness, and be saved on Christ alone, without doing anything meritorious yourself.”
So it is with every sinner.
Tell him to pray for conviction.
Oh yes, he will pray for conviction, but he will resist conviction until he repents.
Tell him to pray for the Holy Spirit.
Oh yes, he will pray for the Holy Spirit, but still he will perhaps resist the Holy Spirit continually.

He is ready to do the outside work, but not the heart-work; he will readily cleanse the outside of the cup and platter, but the turning of his own heart from his sins and selfishness—that is the hard thing, the thing which above all others he is reluctant to do.
Sinners are accustomed to assume, in self-vindication, that it is impossible for them to control their own hearts.
They admit they can control their muscles; if Jesus were on earth, they could come to Him and bow their knees before Him—but they cannot come with their hearts and bow their hearts to Him.
But what is the heart, that you cannot control it?

You are controlling your own hearts all the time, and the very thing God complains of is that you control them too stubbornly, so that His truth and His Spirit cannot move you—that you control them wrongly, and with so much obstinacy as to frustrate all His efforts to save you.
Therefore He cries, “Turn, turn, for why will you die?”

blocks.x: REMARKS.

s: 1. But you ask, “Should not a sinner pray?”
The answer depends on what the question means and implies.
If it means, “Shall a sinner mock God?”
I answer, No. If you mean, “Shall he truly pray, in sincerity and honesty?”
Yes. “Shall he lie to the Holy Spirit?”
No. “Shall he turn to God?” Yes.
But the sum of all that needs to be said on this point is that the sinner should be told to repent and pray—not pray and repent.
Let him observe the scriptural order—an order founded in reason and in the nature of the case.
2. This order of duties is eminently reasonable.
Suppose a sinner had stolen money.
He knows that God is greatly displeased with him for this, and he is also afraid of being detected and disgraced.
Now he says, “What shall I do?”
“Shall I repent and then pray God to forgive me, or shall I pray first?”
Greatly disliking to confess, repent, and restore, he says, “I will do the other thing; I will pray.”
“I will go alone and pray about it, and then perhaps I will repent.”
See him. He takes out his stolen money.
He passes it from one hand to the other. “I am greatly distressed,” he says. “What shall I do?”
“Shall I put it in my pocket and go and pray?”
No, sinner, no. Carry it back—repent first, and then go and pray.
Don’t go and pray for the Holy Spirit first: there is no need of that; the Holy Spirit is already convicting you of your great sin.
Don’t insult Him by refusing to yield to His persuasions, and by pretending to pray for His guidance and help!
Let this represent all sin.
Stealing money is only one form of sin; let it represent all forms of sin.
You, sinner, are fully committed to living for yourself.
You have robbed God by wrenching yourself away from His service.
God says, “Restore. Give yourself back to Me and to My service.”
But you reply, “What shall I do?”
“Shall I not go and pray?”
God says, “Restore first; give back the stolen goods first; then you may pray.”
What should you pray for—until you have restored what you have stolen?
Surely you will not insult God by praying for pardon before you have restored what you have stolen.
You need not pray for the Holy Spirit unless you restore, for to pray and not restore is only resisting and mocking the Spirit of God.
But the sinner says, “You talk as if I could repent.”
Yes, and so does God.
God in His word always speaks as if you could repent, and as if you ought to know that you can.
What if Simon Magus had said, “But you don’t expect me to repent, do you?”
You will notice he said no such thing.
His own conscience neither suggested nor allowed such a defense, nor did the preaching of the apostles encourage it.
But you say, “Does the Bible always assume that I can repent?”
Yes, everywhere—in all its commands—by every prophet, every apostle—by the lips of every forerunner of Christ—by the lips of Christ Himself.
Every inspired command, every inspired direction, holds the same language and makes the same implication.
You can repent, and you ought to do it immediately!
3. When the sinner says, “I can’t repent,” he virtually charges God with being a tyrant.
For what can be a charge of tyranny, if charging God with requiring you to do impossibilities is not?
4. But does not the Bible teach that God gives men repentance?
Yes, and in the same sense as He gives you daily bread—which, however, you must provide yourself and eat yourself.
God does not give you your daily bread as long as you persist in starving yourself.
So God gives you repentance by persuading you to repent—by drawing you—by impressing truth on your heart and conscience.
Indeed, there is no other possible way in which He can give you repentance.
It is only by bringing truth before your mind—impressing it in a thousand ways upon your heart and conscience.
For repentance is a rational, voluntary act—an act done by the sinner because he sees that truth and reason demand it.
5. Every sinner should see and feel that immediate repentance is what God requires.
He should see that he is shut up to precisely this and to nothing else.
Nor is there anything strange or absurd in this.
Suppose a man had committed murder, and you told him to repent of this great sin.
Is there anything mysterious in this?
Or if you see a man engaged in some particular form of wickedness, and you urge him to stop and repent: is there anything strange or unreasonable in this course?
How then can there be anything unreasonable in requiring a sinner to repent of all his sins? Or of that which embraces the sum of all wickedness?

6. Some of you are so afraid that you will repent that you pick up a book, even under the most solemn preaching, and try to keep from thinking of your own sins; and even then you will pretend that you cannot repent, and would gladly imply that you would repent if you could!
Is not this beautifully consistent!
7. Many who profess religion have greatly backslidden from God; they pray in form, yet they don’t repent.
Many talk about praying as if they made up in prayer for what they lack in pleasing God while they go on sinning.
I asked a young lady, “Do you pray?”
“Yes, sir.” “When?” “On going to bed at night.”
“What for?” “That God would take me to heaven if I should die before morning.”
“Do you expect God would do so?”
“No.” “Then you expect to go on in sin.”
Now be honest enough to tell God just the truth.

Say to Him, “Lord, forgive my sins—give me strength by sleep and food so that I may sin a little more; I have sinned all the day past—I don’t intend to repent; I only want to be taken to heaven if I die, for I cannot bear to sink down to hell. Lord, help me to sin on against You as long as I live, and then take me up to heaven!!”
You are shocked; but what shocks you?
Your course, or my language?
There—see the sinner.
He gets on his knees to tell God that he wants repentance, but he lies in saying so, every moment until he actually repents.
And you, backslidden professing Christian, lie to God in every word of your pretended prayer.
Do you say, “I will not repent—I don’t intend to repent”?
If you say anything other than this, you lie to God, for nothing else is true until you actually repent.
The truth is, as long as you continue in your selfish, impenitent state, you don’t mean to repent.
Therefore, let him pray as he will, his true meaning is, “I have no intention of repenting of my sins.”
This is always true until he does repent.
But this praying of sinners in their sins when they do not mean to repent!
Hear him: “O Lord, I implore You to search my heart.”
No, you don’t mean any such thing; you are covering up your own heart all the time.
“O God, come near to me.”
But you are pushing away from God every moment, and as you strive to get away, you only look back over your shoulder and cry to God to reveal His face and draw near to your soul!
Listen—hear what the Bible says.
“Whoever turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be an abomination.”
And what is your course but this?
8. Let me tell you, God is infinitely ready to meet and bless you.
He comes with pardons in His hands—pardons all sealed with blood.
You need only renounce your sins and come to Him; then all will be well.
The very first moment you come before God with a penitent heart, He will meet you with smiles of loving-kindness.
His parable of the prodigal son both illustrates and proves this.
See, the wandering son comes to himself.
Instead of staying away and trying to live on husks, he turns his face toward home, and comes with a confession on his lips and tears of penitence on his cheeks.
He is coming—and now see the aged father.
He spots him in the distance; he recognizes his long-lost son.
See how he leaps from his door and rushes to embrace this returning son.
Oh, how ready! Oh, how much more than merely READY!!
Oh, how ready God is in your case to meet you with the fullest pardon—and wipe all your tears away, and soothe those aching feelings!
Now, dear hearer, don’t go away and say I told you not to pray.
If I told you not to go into your private room, get on your knees, and swear and blaspheme God, could you say with any truth that I told you not to pray?
So I do not teach you not to pray; but I do teach you to be honest.
I warn you, when you pray, not to mock God.
I entreat you, when you pray, to give up your heart to God and repent of all your sin.
When I first repented, I did it on my knees and in the act of prayer.
I knelt down an impenitent sinner, and rose up a penitent.
In the very act of speaking to God, my heart broke; I yielded myself to God.
This is the way.
And do you ask, “Can I believe God?”
Yes. “Can I pray in faith?”
Yes. “Can I give my heart to God in penitence?”
Yes. Why not you as well as Paul—as well as Peter—as well as any one of the myriads who have done this very thing, and in so doing have found mercy?
“For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have everlasting life.” — John 3:16
Sin is the most expensive thing in the universe.
Nothing else can cost so much.
Pardoned or unpardoned, its cost is infinitely great.
If pardoned, the cost falls chiefly on the great atoning substitute; if unpardoned, it must fall on the head of the guilty sinner.
The existence of sin is a fact experienced everywhere—observed everywhere.
There is sin in our race, everywhere, and in dreadful aggravation.
Sin is the violation of an infinitely important law—a law designed and suited to secure the highest good of the universe.
Obedience to this law is by its very nature essential to the good of creatures.
Without obedience there could be no blessedness even in heaven.
Since sin is a violation of a most important law, it cannot be treated lightly.
No government can afford to treat disobedience as a trifle, since everything—the entire welfare of the government and of all the governed—turns on obedience.
The necessity of guarding the law and of punishing disobedience is exactly in proportion to the value of the interests at stake.
The law of God must not be dishonored by anything He does.
It has been dishonored by the disobedience of man; hence all the more need that God should stand by it, to restore its honor.
The utmost dishonor is done to law by disowning, disobeying, and despising it.
Sinful man has done all this.
Therefore, since this law is not only good but intrinsically necessary to the happiness of the governed, it becomes the most necessary thing of all that the lawgiver should vindicate his law.
He must by all means do it.
So sin has involved God’s government in a vast expense.

Either the law must be executed at the expense of the well-being of the whole race, or God must submit to suffer the worst results of disrespect for his law—results which in some form must involve a vast expense.
Take, for example, any human government.
Suppose the righteous and necessary laws it imposes are disowned and dishonored.
In such a case the violated law must be honored by the execution of its penalty, or else something not less costly, and probably much more so, must be endured.
Transgression must cost happiness somewhere, and in vast amount.
In the case of God’s government it has been judged wise to provide a substitute, one who would serve the purpose of saving the sinner and yet of honoring the law.
Once this was determined, the next great question was: How shall the expense be met?
The Bible tells us how the question was in fact decided.
By a voluntary conscription—shall I call it that—or a donation?
Call it what we may, it was a voluntary offering.
Who will head the subscription list?
Who will begin, where so much is to be raised?
Who will make the first sacrifice?
Who will take the first step in a project so vast?
The Bible tells us.
It began with the Infinite Father.
He made the first great donation.
He gave his only begotten Son—this to begin with—and having given him first, He freely gives everything else that the needs of the case can require.
First He gave his Son to make the atonement due to the law; then He gave and sent his Holy Spirit to take charge of this work.
The Son, for his part, consented to stand as the representative of sinners, that he might honor the law by suffering in their place.

He poured out his blood and made a whole life of suffering a free offering on the altar—he did not hide his face from spitting, nor his back from lashes—he did not shrink from the utmost scorn that wicked men could heap on him.
So the Holy Spirit also devotes himself unceasingly to the most self-denying efforts to accomplish the great object.

It would have been a very short method to have turned his hand against the wicked of our race and sent them all down quickly to hell, as he once did when certain angels “did not keep their first estate.”
Rebellion broke out in heaven.
God did not bear it long around his lofty throne.

But in the case of man he changed his course—he did not send them all to hell, but devised a vast plan of measures, involving the most amazing self-denials and self-sacrifices, to win men’s souls back to obedience and heaven.
For whom was this great donation made?
“God so loved the world,” meaning the whole race of men.
By “the world” in this connection cannot be meant only some particular part, but the whole race.
Not only the Bible but the nature of the case shows that the atonement must have been made for the whole world.

For plainly, if it had not been made for the entire race, no man of the race could ever know that it was made for himself, and therefore not one man could believe in Christ in the sense of receiving by faith the blessings of the atonement. Since there would be complete uncertainty about the persons included in the limited provision we are now supposing, the entire donation must fail, because rational faith to receive it would be impossible.
Suppose a rich man makes a will bequeathing certain property to certain unknown persons, described only by the name “the elect.”

They are described in no other way than by this term, and all agree that although the maker of the will had the individuals definitely in mind, he left no description of them that either the persons themselves, the courts, or any living mortal can understand.
Now such a will is necessarily altogether null and void.
No living man can claim under such a will, and it would be none the better even if these elect were described as residents of Oberlin.
Since it does not include all the residents of Oberlin, and does not define which of them, all is lost.
All having an equal claim and none having any definite claim, none can inherit.
If the atonement were made in this way, no living man would have any valid reason for believing himself one of the elect before he received the gospel.
Hence he would have no authority to believe and to receive its blessings by faith.
In fact, on this supposition, the atonement must be wholly void unless a special revelation is made to the persons for whom it is intended.
As the case actually stands, however, the very fact that a man belongs to the race of Adam—the fact that he is human, born of woman—is entirely sufficient.
It brings him within the boundary.
He is one of the world for whom God gave his Son, that whoever would believe in him might not perish but have everlasting life.
The inner motive in the mind of God for this great gift was love, love for the world.
God so loved the world that he gave his Son to die for it.
God loved the universe also, but this gift of his Son sprang from love for our world.
True, in this great act he took pains to provide for the interests of the universe.
He was careful to do nothing that could in the least lower the sacredness of his law.
He intended most carefully to guard against any misunderstanding of his regard for his law and for the high interests of obedience and happiness in his moral universe.
He meant, once for all, to rule out the danger that any moral agent should be tempted to undervalue the moral law.
Further still, it was not only from love for souls, but from respect for the spirit of the law of his own eternal reason, that he gave up his Son to die.
