It was in this that the purpose to give up his Son originated.
The law of his own reason must be honored and held sacred.
He may do nothing inconsistent with its spirit.
He must do everything possible to prevent the commission of sin and to secure the confidence and love of his subjects.
So sacred did he hold these great objects that he would baptize his Son in his own blood sooner than endanger the good of the universe.
Beyond question, it was love and regard for the highest good of the universe that led him to sacrifice his own beloved Son.
Let us next consider attentively the nature of this love.
The text lays special stress on this—God so loved—his love was of such a nature, so wonderful and so unique in its character, that it led him to give up his only Son to die.
Clearly, more is implied in this expression than simply its greatness.
It is most distinctive in its character.

Unless we understand this, we will be in danger of falling into the strange mistake of the Universalists, who are forever talking about God’s love for sinners, but whose ideas of the nature of this love never lead to repentance or to holiness.

They seem to think of this love as mere good nature, and conceive of God only as a very good-natured being whom nobody needs to fear. Such notions have not the least influence toward holiness, but the very opposite.
It is only when we come to understand what this love is in its nature that we feel its moral power promoting holiness.
It may reasonably be asked: If God so loved the world with a love marked by greatness, and by greatness only, why did He not save all the world without sacrificing his Son?
This question is enough to show us that there is deep meaning in this word “so,” and it should lead us to a careful study of this meaning.
1. This love in its nature is not complacency—a delight in the character of the race.
This could not be, for there was nothing lovable in their character.
For God to have loved such a race with complacent delight would have been infinitely disgraceful to himself.
2. It was not a mere emotion or feeling.
It was not a blind impulse, though many seem to suppose it was.
It seems often to be supposed that God acted as men do when they are carried away by strong emotion.
But there could be no virtue in this.
A man might give away all he is worth under such a blind impulse of feeling and be none the more virtuous.
But in saying this we do not exclude all emotion from the love of benevolence, nor from God’s love for a lost world.
He had emotion, but not emotion only.
Indeed, the Bible everywhere teaches us that God’s love for man, lost in his sins, was paternal—the love of a father for his offspring—in this case, for rebellious, perverse, prodigal offspring.
In this love, of course, the deepest compassion must be blended.
3. On the part of Christ, considered as Mediator, this love was paternal.
“He is not ashamed to call them brothers.”
From one point of view he is acting for brothers, and from another, for children.
The Father gave him up for this work, and of course shares in the love appropriate to its relationships.
4. This love must be entirely disinterested, for he had nothing to hope for or to fear—no profit to make from his children if they should be saved.
Indeed, it is impossible to conceive of God as selfish, since his love embraces all creatures and all interests according to their real value.
No doubt he took delight in saving our race—why should he not?
It is a great salvation in every sense, and it greatly swells the bliss of heaven; it will greatly affect the glory and the blessedness of the Infinite God.
He will eternally respect himself for love so disinterested.
He also knows that all his holy creatures will eternally respect him for this work and for the love that gave birth to it.
But let it also be said that he knew they would not respect him for this great work unless they saw that he did it for the good of sinners.
5. This love was zealous—not that cold-hearted state of mind that some suppose, not an abstraction, but a love that is deep, zealous, earnest, burning in his soul like a fire that nothing can quench.
6. The sacrifice was a most self-denying one.
Did it cost the Father nothing to give up his own beloved Son to suffer, and to die such a death?
If this is not self-denial, what can be?
To give up his Son in this way to so much suffering—is this not the noblest self-denial?
The universe could never have had the idea of great self-denial except for such an example.
7. This love was particular because it was universal, and also universal because it was particular.
God loved each sinner in particular, and therefore loved all.
Because he loved all impartially, without favoritism, he therefore loved each in particular.
8. This was a most patient love.
How rare it is to find a parent who so loves his child as never to be impatient!

Let me go around and ask: how many of you parents can say that you love all your children so well, with so much love, and with a love so wisely controlling, that you have never felt impatient toward any of them—so that you can take them in your arms under the greatest provocations and love them down, love them out of their sins, love them into repentance and into a filial spirit?
Of which of your children can you say, “Thank God, I never fretted against that child”? Of which, if you were to meet him in heaven, could you say, “I never caused that child to fret”?
Often I have heard parents say, “I love my children, but oh, how my patience fails me!”
And after the dear ones are dead you may hear their bitter moans: “O my soul, how could I have caused my child so much stumbling and so much sin!”
But God never frets—he is never impatient.
His love is so deep and so great that he is always patient.

Sometimes when parents have unfortunate children, poor objects of compassion, they can bear anything from them; but when their children are very wicked, they seem to feel quite excused for being impatient.
In God’s case, these are not unfortunate children, but intensely wicked, intelligently wicked.

But oh, his amazing patience—so set on their good, so desirous of their highest welfare, that however they abuse Him, He sets himself to bless them still, and weep them down, and bleed them down, and die them down by the death of his Son in their place!
9. This is a jealous love, not in a bad sense but in a good sense—in the sense of being exceedingly careful lest anything should happen to injure those he loves.
It is just as a husband and wife who truly love each other are jealous with ever-wakeful jealousy over each other’s welfare, always seeking to do all they can to promote each other’s true interests.
This donation has already been made—made in good faith—not only promised, but actually made.
The promise, given long before, has been fulfilled.
The Son has come—he has died, has paid the ransom, and lives to offer it—a salvation prepared for all who will embrace it.
The Son of God did not die to appease vengeance, as some seem to understand it, but under the demands of law.
The law had been dishonored by its violation.
Therefore Christ undertook to honor it by yielding up to its demands his suffering life and atoning death.
It was not to appease a vindictive spirit in God, but to secure the highest good of the universe in a dispensation of mercy.
Since this atonement has been made, all men in the race have a right to it.
It is open to everyone who will embrace it.

Though Jesus still remains the Father’s Son, yet by gracious right he belongs in an important sense to the race—to everyone—so that every sinner has an interest in his blood if he will only come humbly forward and claim it.
God sent his Son to be the Savior of the world—of whoever would believe and accept this great salvation.
God gives his Spirit to apply this salvation to men.
He comes to each man’s door and knocks, to gain entrance if he can, and to show each sinner that he may have salvation now.
Oh, what a labor of love this is!
This salvation must be received, if at all, by faith.
This is the only possible way.
God’s government over sinners is moral, not physical, because the sinner himself is a moral and not a physical agent.
Therefore God can influence us in no way unless we give him our confidence.
He can never save us merely by taking us away to some place called heaven—as if a change of place would change the voluntary heart.
There can, therefore, be no possible way to be saved but by simple faith.
Now do not be mistaken and suppose that embracing the gospel is simply believing these historical facts without truly receiving Christ as your Savior.
If this had been the plan, then Christ would have needed only to come down and die, then go back to heaven and quietly wait to see who would believe the facts.
But how different the real case is!
Now Christ comes down to fill the soul with his own life and love.
Penitent sinners hear and believe the truth about Jesus, and then receive Christ into the soul to live and reign there supreme and forever.
On this point many are mistaken, saying, “If I believe the facts as matters of history, that is enough.”
No! No! That is not it by any means.
“It is with the heart that man believes unto righteousness.”

The atonement was indeed made to provide the way, so that Jesus could come down to human hearts and draw them into union and sympathy with himself—so that God could reach down the arms of his love and embrace sinners—so that law and government would not be dishonored by such tokens of friendship shown by God toward sinners.
But the atonement will by no means save sinners except as it prepares the way for them to come into sympathy and fellowship of heart with God.
Now Jesus comes to each sinner’s door and knocks—listen—what’s that? What’s that?
Why this knocking? Why did He not go away and stay in heaven, if that were the system, until men should simply believe the historical facts and be baptized for salvation, as some suppose?

But now, see how He comes down—tells the sinner what He has done—reveals all his love—tells him how holy and sacred it is, so sacred that He can by no means act without regard to the holiness of his law and the purity of his government.
Thus, impressing on the heart the deepest and broadest ideas of his holiness and purity, He presses home the need of deep repentance and the sacred duty of renouncing all sin.

blocks.x: REMARKS.

s: 1. The Bible teaches that sinners may forfeit their birthright and put themselves beyond the reach of mercy.
Not long ago I made some remarks to you on the evident necessity that God should guard himself against the abuses of his love.
The circumstances are such as to create the greatest danger of such abuse, and therefore He must make sinners know that they may not abuse his love, and cannot do it with impunity.
2. Under the gospel, sinners are in circumstances of the greatest possible responsibility.
They are in the utmost danger of trampling the very Son of God under their feet.
“Come,” they say, “let us kill Him, and the inheritance will be ours.”
When God sends out, last of all, his own beloved Son, what do they do?
They add to all their other sins and rebellions the highest insult to this glorious Son!
Suppose something similar to this were done under a human government.
A rebellion breaks out in some of the provinces.

The king sends his own son, not with an army to cut them down swiftly in their rebellion, but gently, meekly, patiently he goes among them, explaining the laws of the kingdom and urging them to obedience.
What do they do in that case?
With one accord they combine to seize him and put him to death!
But you deny that this applies, and ask me, “Who murdered the Son of God?”
“Were they not Jews?”
Yes, and have you sinners had no part in this murder?
Has not your treatment of Jesus Christ shown that you are fully in sympathy with the ancient Jews in their murder of the Son of God?
If you had been there, would anyone have shouted louder than you, “Away with him—crucify him, crucify him”?
Have you not always said, “Depart from us, for we do not wish to know Your ways”?
3. It was said of Christ that though He was rich, He became poor, that we through his poverty might be rich.
How strikingly true this is!
Our redemption cost Christ his life; it found Him rich but made Him poor; it found us infinitely poor but made us rich, even to all the wealth of heaven.
But none can share in these riches until each one for himself accepts them in the rightful way.
They must be received on the terms proposed, or the offer passes away completely, and you are left poorer even than if no such treasures had ever been laid at your feet.
Many people seem to misunderstand this case entirely.
They seem not to believe what God says, but keep saying, “If, if, if there were only any salvation for me—if only there were an atonement provided for the pardon of my sins.”
This was one of the last things that was cleared up in my mind before I fully committed my soul to trust God.

I had been studying the atonement; I saw its philosophical bearings—saw what it demanded of the sinner; but it irritated me, and I said, “If I should become a Christian, how could I know what God would do with me?”

Under this irritation I said foolish and bitter things against Christ—until my own soul was horrified at its own wickedness, and I said, “I will make all this right with Christ, if the thing is possible.”
In this way many advance on the encouragements of the gospel as if it were only a “perhaps,” an experiment.
They take each step forward most carefully, with fear and trembling, as if there were the utmost doubt whether there could be any mercy for them.
So it was with me. I was on my way to my office when the question came before my mind: “What are you waiting for?”
“You need not make such a fuss.”
“All is done already.”
“You have only to consent to the proposal—give your heart right up to it at once—this is all.”
That is just how it is.

All Christians and sinners ought to understand that the whole plan is complete—that the whole of Christ, his character, his work, his atoning death, and his ever-living intercession, belongs to each and every man, and needs only to be accepted.
There is a full ocean of it.
There it is. You may just as well take it as not.

It is as if you stood on the shore of an ocean of soft, pure water, perishing with thirst; you are welcome to drink, and you need not fear that you will exhaust that ocean, or cause anybody else to go without by drinking yourself.
You need not feel that you are not given free access to that ocean of waters; you are invited and urged to drink—yes, to drink abundantly!
This ocean supplies all your need.
You do not need to have the attributes of Jesus Christ in yourself, for his attributes become practically yours for every possible use.
As the Scripture says, He has been made to us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.
What do you need?
Wisdom? Here it is.
Righteousness? Here it is.
Sanctification? Here you have it.
All is in Christ.
Can you possibly think of any one thing needed for your moral purity or your usefulness that is not here in Christ?
Nothing. All is provided here.
Therefore you need not say, “I will go and pray and try,” as in the hymn—
There is no need for any “perhaps.”
The doors are always open.

They are like the doors of Broadway Tabernacle in New York, made to swing open and fasten themselves open, so that they could not swing back and shut on the crowds of people thronging to pass through.
When they were to be made, I went to the workmen myself and told them by all means to fix them so that they would swing open and fasten themselves in that position.
So the door of salvation is always open—fastened open, and no man can shut it—not even the Pope, nor the devil, nor any angel from heaven or from hell.
There it stands, swung all the way back, and the passage wide open for every sinner of our race to enter if he will.
Again, sin is the most expensive thing in the universe.
Are you well aware, O sinner, what a price has been paid for you, that you may be redeemed and made an heir of God and of heaven?
Oh, what an expensive business it is for you to indulge in sin!
And what an enormous tax the government of God has paid to redeem this province from its ruin!
Talk about the poor tax of Great Britain, with that of all other nations added on—all is nothing compared to the sin-tax of Jehovah’s government—that awful sin-tax!
Think how much machinery is kept in motion to save sinners!

The Son of God was sent down; angels are sent as ministering spirits to the heirs of salvation; missionaries are sent; Christians labor and pray and weep in deep and anxious concern—all to seek and save the lost.
What a wonderful—what an enormous—tax is levied on the benevolence of the universe to put away sin and to save the sinner!
If the cost could be computed in solid gold, what a world of it there would be—a solid globe in itself!
What an array of toil and cost, from angels, Jesus Christ, the Divine Spirit, and living men!
Shame on sinners who hold on to sin in spite of all these benevolent efforts to save them!—who, instead of being shamed out of sin, will say, “Let God pay off this tax—who cares!”
“Let the missionaries labor, let godly women work their very fingers off to raise funds to keep all this human machinery in motion; no matter—what is all this to me?”
“I have loved my pleasures, and after them I will go!”
What an unfeeling heart this is!
Sinners can very well afford to make sacrifices to save their fellow sinners.
Paul could, for his fellow sinners.
He felt that he had done his part toward making sinners, and now it was fitting for him to do his part also in converting them back to God.
But look there—that young man thinks he cannot afford to be a minister, because he is afraid he will not be well supported.
Does he not owe something to the grace that saved his soul from hell?
Has he not some sacrifices to make, since Jesus has made so many for him—and Christians too, in Christ before him—did they not pray and suffer and toil for his soul’s salvation?
As for his danger of lacking bread in the Lord’s work, let him trust his Great Master.
Yet let me also say that churches may be greatly at fault for not supporting their pastors comfortably.
Let them know that God will surely starve them if they starve their ministers.
Their own souls and the souls of their children will be as barren as death if they greedily starve those whom God in his providence sends to feed them with the bread of life.
How much it costs to rid society of certain forms of sin—for example, slavery!
How much has already been spent, and how much more still remains to be spent before this grievous evil and curse and sin is rooted out of our land!
This is part of God’s great enterprise, and He will press it on to its completion.
Yet at what an amazing cost!
How many lives and how much agony to get rid of this one sin!
Woe to those who make profit out of the sins of men!
Just think of the rumseller—tempting men while God is trying to dissuade them from rushing on in the ways of sin and death!
Think of the guilt of those who in this way set themselves in battle array against God!
So Christ has to contend with rumsellers who are doing all they can to hinder his work.
Our subject strikingly illustrates the nature of sin as mere selfishness.

It does not care how much sin costs Jesus Christ—how much it costs the church, how much it taxes the benevolent sympathies and the self-sacrificing labors of all the good on earth or in heaven—no matter; the sinner loves self-indulgence and will have it while he can.
How many of you have cost your friends countless tears and trouble to bring you back from your sinful ways?
Are you not ashamed, when so much has been done for you, that you cannot be persuaded to give up your sins and turn to God and holiness?
The whole effort on God’s part for man is one of suffering and self-denial.
Beginning with the sacrifice of his own beloved Son, it is carried on with ever-renewed sacrifices and toilsome labors—at great and wonderful expense.

Just think how long these efforts have already been prolonged—how many tears, poured out like water, it has cost—how much pain in many forms this enterprise has caused and cost—yes, that very sin which you roll as a sweet morsel under your tongue!
God may well hate it when He sees how much it costs, and say, “Oh, do not do this abominable thing that I hate!”
Yet God is not unhappy in these self-denials.
So great is his joy in the results that He considers all the suffering comparatively a trifle, just as earthly parents enjoy the efforts they make to bless their children.

Look at them; they will almost work their very hands off—mothers sit up at night plying their needles until they reel with fatigue and blindness—but if you were to see their toil, you would often see their joy as well, so intensely do they love their children.
Such is the labor, the joy, and the self-denial of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in their great work for human salvation.
Often they are grieved that so many will refuse to be saved.
Toiling on in a common sympathy, there is nothing, within reasonable limits, that they will not do or suffer to accomplish their great work.
It is wonderful to think how all creation also sympathizes in this work and its necessary sufferings.
Go back to the scene of Christ’s sufferings.
Could the sun in the heavens look down unmoved on such a scene?
Oh no, he could not even behold it—he veiled his face from the sight!
All nature seemed to put on her robes of deepest mourning.
The scene was too much even for inanimate nature to bear.
The sun turned his back and could not look down on such a spectacle!
The subject forcefully illustrates the worth of the soul.
Do you think God would have done all this if he had held those low views on this subject that sinners usually have?
Martyrs and saints enjoy their sufferings—filling up in themselves what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ; not in the atonement proper, but in the subordinate parts of the work to be done.
It is the nature of true religion to love self-denial.
The results will fully justify all the expense.
God had counted the cost well before He began.
Long before He formed a moral universe, He knew perfectly what it must cost him to redeem sinners, and He knew that the result would amply justify all the cost.
He knew that a wonder of mercy would be accomplished—that the suffering demanded of Christ, great as it was, would be endured; and that infinitely glorious results would come from it.

He looked down the track of time into the distant ages—where, as the cycles rolled on, the joys of redeemed saints might be seen, as they sing their songs and strike their harps anew with the everlasting song through the long, long, LONG eternity of their blessedness—and was not this enough for the heart of infinite love to enjoy?
And what do you think of it, Christian?
Will you say now, “I am ashamed to ask to be forgiven”?
“How can I bear to receive such mercy!”
“It is the price of blood, and how can I accept it?”
“How can I put Jesus to so much expense?”

You are right in saying that you have cost Him great expense—but the expense has been cheerfully met—the pain has all been endured and will not need to be endured again, and it will cost no more if you accept than if you decline; and moreover, let it be considered that Jesus Christ has not acted unwisely; he did not pay too much for the soul’s redemption—not one pang more than the interests of God’s government demanded and the worth of the soul would justify.

Oh, when you come to see him face to face and tell Him what you think of it—when you are some thousands of years older than you are now—will you not adore that wisdom that manages this plan, and the infinite love in which it had its birth?
Oh, what will you say then of that amazing condescension that brought Jesus down to your rescue!

Tell me, Christian, have you not often poured out your soul before your Savior in acknowledgment of what you have cost Him, and there seemed to be a kind of lifting up, as if the very bottom of your soul were about to rise, and you would pour out your whole heart?
If anybody had seen you, they would have wondered what had happened to you that had so melted your soul in gratitude and love.
Tell me now, sinners, will you sell your birthright?
How much will you take for it?
How much will you take for your interest in Christ?
For how much will you sell your soul?
Sell your Christ! Of old they sold Him for thirty pieces of silver; and ever since, the heavens have been raining tears of blood on our guilty world.
If the devil were to ask you to fix the sum for which you would sell your soul, what price would you name?
Lorenzo Dow once met a man as he was riding along a lonely road to keep an appointment, and said to him, “Friend, have you ever prayed?”
“No.” “How much will you take never to pray from now on?”
“One dollar.” Dow paid it over and rode on.
The man put the money in his pocket and went on, thinking.
The more he thought, the worse he felt.
“There,” he said, “I have sold my soul for one dollar!”
“It must be that I have met the devil!”
“Nobody else would tempt me like this.”
“With all my soul I must repent or be damned forever!”
How often have you bargained to sell your Savior for less than thirty pieces of silver!
No, for the merest trifle!
Finally, God wants volunteers to help on this great work.
God has given himself, and given his Son, and sent his Spirit—but more laborers are still needed; and what will you give?
Paul said, “I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.”
Do you aspire to such an honor?
What will you do—what will you suffer?
Do not say, “I have nothing to give.”
You can give yourself—your eyes, your ears, your hands, your mind, your heart, everything; and surely nothing you have is too sacred and too good to be devoted to such a work at such a call!
How many young men are ready to go? And how many young women?
Whose heart leaps up, crying, “Here am I! Send me”?
“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” Matthew 5:7
What is mercy? And who are the merciful?
These are properly the first questions to be considered.
Mercy is not to be confused with goodness, since it is only an attribute of goodness.
Justice is another, but justice stands in some respects opposite to mercy.
Goodness is the more comprehensive term, and includes both mercy and justice.
Justice treats moral agents according to their character and what they deserve; mercy treats them better than this, and would do them all the good she can, in spite of their ill-desert.
Thus God sends rain on the unjust as well as on the just, doing good to those who deserve none.
Justice would execute the law; but mercy sets aside its execution wherever she can do so with reasonable safety.
Justice is apparently exacting, and omits all efforts to bless the guilty, but makes them a sacrifice to the public good, being in these respects quite distinct from and even opposite to mercy.
Mercy would persevere in efforts to do the sinner good; she would be forbearing even toward enemies.
Christ commends the exercise of mercy.
If, he says, you love only those who love you, what thanks do you deserve?
And if you do good to those who do good to you, what thanks do you deserve?
Do not even the tax collectors do the same?
In this, what do you do more than others?
The special manifestations of mercy and justice take on certain peculiar aspects in one who acts as a ruler.
Justice becomes more imperative; it may not be up to him to exercise mercy wherever he would like.
His office demands of him a sacred regard for the general interests of the community.
These remarks apply to God in his relations as the moral Governor of our race.
Those relations bind him to infinite watchfulness over his kingdom, to secure due respect for the law and the great Lawgiver.
But God does not hinder his creatures in the exercise of mercy by placing on them the execution of retributive justice under his government.
He knows they are not competent for that responsibility.
It is good that we are not required to bear it.
We are now left free to forgive our enemies and to exercise almost unlimited mercy toward them.
“Vengeance belongs to God,” and he knows how and when to administer it.
But we are fully at liberty to seek their good and nothing but their good, except where God, or the demands of society, may make an exception.
You are aware that in some very peculiar circumstances God has forbidden his people to seek the good of the wicked.
Of the Ammonite and Moabite, God said (Deut. 23:6), “You shall not seek their peace nor their prosperity all your days forever.”
When God comes forth to execute his law on nations, it removes them from the reach of our mercy.
So when he sends sinners to hell, bringing them there under the perfect execution of his retributive justice, we can pray for them no longer, and may no longer seek their peace.
But, universally, unless God forbids us to seek their good, we should seek it earnestly.
We are to have a merciful disposition always.
God has. We may truly say of him that the attribute of mercy in his heart is always alive—always boiling up from its deep, eternal fountain.
He is never malicious, not even toward his bitterest enemies in hell.

He would speak as kindly as Abraham is represented as speaking in the parable—“Son, remember that in your lifetime you received your good things”—where every word is spoken with all the kindness the circumstances allow.
So human magistrates often hold back their tender emotions.
Their hearts are full of love, but their responsibilities compel them to administer justice, for under God they are “ministers of wrath” to carry out his sentence against evildoers.
Let us note here a very obvious distinction between the magistrate and the man.
As a man and in his personal relations, the judge may treat the prisoner with the tenderest compassion, while as judge he still firmly sentences him to a shameful death.

The sheriff may strike the fatal blow that releases the drop with a steady hand, but faint suddenly afterward under the fearful shock it gives his nerves to send a guilty man suddenly into the eternal world.
As a man, he is merciful; as an officer, he is bound to be just.
When we read the New Testament we are struck by its broad requirements to be merciful.
In the Lord’s Prayer, we are taught to pray, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors,” as if we need not expect mercy from God any further than we show mercy to our fellow men.
If my brother sins against me, someone said, how often shall I forgive him?
Up to seven times? No, Jesus replied, but “up to seventy times seven.”
It is your concern always to seek the good of your enemies and to treat them in every case with lovingkindness.
On this our Lord lays great stress, always putting strong cases and requiring this spirit toward all, friends and enemies.
What is implied in forgiveness?
In God it implies setting aside the penalty of the law.
But it cannot imply this in our case, since we do not have this responsibility.
A pardon under any government sets aside the legal disabilities that the offense created.
But in our private capacity, it is only a loving spirit and cheerful expressions of favor and goodwill.
Suppose you have been wronged.
What does mercy then imply in your case?
That you try to reform the offender, and try to save him from the penalty of the law of God, under which he must sink to hell unless he repents.
Persistent efforts to do him good make up the true idea.
This is our duty to personal enemies.
So Christ teaches us to bless those who curse us, to do good to those who do evil to us.
To do this, and to persevere in loving efforts to save them, is mercy.
Our Lord urges on his people the exercise of mercy in many forms and with wonderful energy and fullness.
“You have heard that it has been said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’
But I say to you that you do not resist evil; but whoever strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also.”
He insists that we are not to avenge ourselves or retaliate, but are to go the full length of mercy.
In these beatitudes, Christ commanded those forms of virtue that are among the most difficult for depraved human nature.
If we compare these with other forms of what we call virtue, we will see the force of this remark.
For example, we regard hatred of sin, a sense of justice, and an approval of retribution as forms of virtue.
But they are almost natural, even to depraved hearts.
It is natural to hate sin—all but our own, and perhaps even those; certainly we cannot approve of them.
Men can never love sin for its own sake.
They love it for the good, though fleeting, that they hope to gain from it.
Who can take any pleasure in the character of the devil?
No man can approve of real malice.
This is the reason why you see outbreaks of violence and summary proceedings under lynch law.
A striking example was provided a few years ago in a case where a steamboat captain violated a young lady entrusted to his care.

When his trial came on at Buffalo, his defense seemed determined to make very light of his crime, and even the magistrate was thought to be conniving at this strategy; whereupon public indignation was so aroused that the people threatened to tear down his office, and did compel him to administer justice in the case.
Hardly any men could be found who would tolerate that sort of crime.
The virtue implied in such indignation against sin is comparatively easy.
But these virtues, commended in Matthew 5, are real and difficult.
Perhaps they are the only sure tests of a regenerate heart.
If these are absent, the evidence must be deficient.
There is a kind of compassion for the offender that makes excuses for sin, looking to the protection of the criminal from punishment, and not to the protection of society from outrage.
It cares much about shielding the guilty, and little about promoting the interests of peace and purity.
We often see such a spirit among Universalists.
All their sympathies tend to go with the sinner.
They throw their influence in the way of the administration of justice.
Where Universalism prevails, it often happens that you cannot get a jury to convict for a capital crime.
Clearly, this spirit is not with, but against, the law of God.
It is easy and natural enough for those who intend and hope to escape all punishment themselves to take sides with criminals.
A merciful disposition is never inclined to take sides with sin and the sinner against what is right.
You see this in the spirit that moved God to send Jesus Christ to die for sinners in order to magnify the law and honor his throne.
You also see the same thing in the spirit that Jesus himself showed.
Both always defended the divine law, and most fully honored and upheld it.
Christ came to condemn the sin of the world and not to excuse it or justify it.
Because he condemned it, he laid down his life for it.
He would not ask that sinners be forgiven until he had fully honored and satisfied the law by his own death in the sinner’s place.

It is a curious fact that that whole class of men, the Universalists, who throw their influence against the administration of the law on criminals, set aside the atonement made by the death of Christ.
They do not recognize the principle on which it rests.
They do not believe in sacrificing anybody’s happiness for the sake of upholding law and government.
What if Christ had been of their mind and had acted on their principle?
Then there would have been no salvation for our race.
Mercifulness has no sympathy with sin and never covers it up from view.
Guilt is a precondition for the exercise of mercy.
The idea of mercy presupposes the fact of guilt.
No one can be an object of mercy except as he deserves punishment.
If the ill-desert is small in amount, there is room for the exercise of only a little mercy.
If a man deserves three years in the State Prison, mercy can pardon him for three years only.
The greater the virtue of mercifulness, the richer its reward.
When exercised under appropriate circumstances, it surely brings intense happiness, but if we exercise justice where the case demands mercy, we miss the reward.
The exercise of justice also, where the case demands it, brings real happiness, but mercy in its appropriate place brings much more.
We are all aware that when we exercise mercy rightly, it is a special gratification to us, far above what we feel in the exercise of justice.
If the public good demands the execution of justice, we enjoy it, but wherever the case will allow the exercise of mercy, there is great luxury in it.

blocks.x: REMARKS.

s: How sublime and wonderful is the mercifulness of God!
Just think what moral grandeur is shown in his mercy toward our world!
He is not only patient and forbearing, in spite of our great iniquities, but he loads us down with favors.
Then think also at what cost to himself.
Suppose a man had injured you and had continued to heap wrongs on you for a long time; but you freely pardon him, even at great cost.
You give your money, your time, and your labor to provide the necessary means of obtaining his pardon, and finally you even lay down your life for him.
Would you not think this a wonderful case of love?
But, by a most wonderful manifestation, God gave his Son to die for sinners, showing how greatly he delighted in mercy and that judgment is his “strange work.”
This exercise of rich mercy must have gratified Jesus Christ.
Those of us who have shown mercy toward people who have abused us can appreciate this.
We can understand that Jesus must find the richest and most intense satisfaction in the exercise of his great mercy toward sinners.
It is by his manifested love that God overcomes the hearts of his enemies.

Revealing his great love, he subdues their hearts and brings them under this power of love; and then, though they deserve to be banished forever, he rejoices over them as one who has found great spoil.
As when the prodigal son returned, starving and filthy, but penitent, the father is seen rushing out to meet him, his heart overflowing with joy.
If we may judge the happiness of heaven from our own experience, we must conclude that God’s most intense happiness is found in the exercise of mercy, and that this is his highest form of virtue.
The exercise of mercy has always been a present intention with him, and in this sense, a present reality.
God’s mercifulness must greatly strengthen his influence and power as moral Governor.
Angels desire to look into this plan of redeeming mercy.

They were alert to its first hints, and as soon as it began to unfold, they caught up the glorious idea, and all the heavenly host took wing, rushing down to earth to join in the swelling notes of the first great anthem—“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth, peace and goodwill toward men!”
Who can doubt that this manifestation greatly increased their happiness and also their holiness—their love of God and their joy in his reign?
This manifestation of God’s mercy must confound Satan and all hell.
What can they say when they see the cost at which God exercises mercy!
How confounded they must be when they see how their plan to overthrow God’s empire by bringing sin into our world has served mainly to strengthen it, through his glorious manifestations of mercy!
Some have wondered why God did not annihilate Adam and Eve as soon as they fell through sin.
The fact is, he could not afford to.
By that event, an opportunity was given him to do a great work for his kingdom.
It was a glorious opportunity, and he could not afford to lose it.
Mercy was a rich and glorious attribute of his nature, and the time had now come to manifest it on a wondrous scale.
In the case of the fallen angels, he had manifested his justice and its fearful forms; but an ocean of mercy was boiling up from the depths of his heart, and how could it be suppressed any longer?
Why should he any longer give up the luxury of exercising it?
Luxury, do I say?
Certainly. So great is his mercy that no luxury can be compared to this.
Do you suppose he feels it a sacrifice and an unhappiness to show mercy to lost men?
No indeed. It is no less true of him than of us—“Blessed is the merciful!”
Those who have not forgiven all men from their hearts are not themselves forgiven.
I have sometimes seen people in great distress of mind for a long time, and have asked them, “Are there not people whom you regard as your enemies and whom you will not forgive?”
In many cases, this has been the obvious reason why they cannot find mercy.
It is very common for people to linger long under conviction of sin and in great anxiety, utterly unable to find peace because they do not forgive their supposed enemies.
Some years ago we had among us a poor Black man who, as he came near death, was greatly troubled about his preparation.
I said to him, “Do you forgive all your enemies?”
“No,” he said, “by no means; I have been robbed almost all my life of my liberty, my labor, and my very life, and how can I ever forgive the men who have done all this?
If I cannot be saved without forgiving my enemies, then I must be lost!”
I found him in this state several times and labored to show him his duty.
At length, as I entered his room on one occasion, I saw his face glowing with joy and peace.
As soon as he saw me, he cried out, “I’ve gotten over it; God has helped me over it; I love my enemies now!”
He was indeed a new man and died in the blessed peace of the gospel.
Some say, “I can forgive but cannot forget.”
Probably they do not really forgive.
Many get a hope and deceive themselves.
They do not fully and heartily forgive their enemies, and neither does God forgive them.
Sometimes men say, “If those who have injured me have repented, I can forgive them—not otherwise.”
That is not the right ground.
God will take care of their repentance before him, and can judge its sincerity far better than you can.
He does not place on you the responsibility of finding out whether your enemy is truly penitent or not.
All he asks of you is to have a merciful spirit toward him.
That is your part.
The gospel is an illustration of the spirit of the law, for the law requires the exercise of mercy because it requires perfect benevolence, and this of course involves mercy.
In his death for sinners, Christ gave us the true meaning of the law of God in its spirituality.
The gospel therefore is not contrary to the law, but illustrates it truly and beautifully.
God’s character as seen in the gospel is like his character as seen in the law, except that the latter omits some manifestations made in the former.
The manifestations are similar as far as the comparison extends.
You have more in the gospel than in the law, but nothing contradictory—nothing inconsistent in the one compared with the other.
The Jews in Christ’s time had a very low estimate of the law.
Therefore Christ needed to labor hard to raise the law above their standard.
We see this running through most of his sermons on the mount.
The whole system of forgiveness and love of enemies assumed a higher standard.
Christ taught men not to resist evil, but to exercise the utmost forbearance and mercifulness.
Repeatedly Christ said, in substance: You teach a virtue common to saints and to sinners—doing good only to those who do good to you.
I come to give you new and higher conceptions of virtue.
There is a state of feeling that resembles mercy and is often mistaken for it, but falls short of it.
Christ alludes to it when he says, “If you love those who love you, what reward do you have?”
It is a partial mercifulness—exercising forbearance toward those we love and who are perhaps related to us by special ties.
But this is not real mercy.
Benevolence is the love of everybody—it extends to all.
You do not show mercifulness while you love only particular persons and there are some toward whom you have no forgiving spirit.
As long as there is one person for whom you cannot pray, it is plain there is one whom you do not sincerely love.
If you are in such a state of mind that you cannot labor affectionately for his salvation, you prove yourself to be radically wrong.
For you are bound to forgive all.
Otherwise, how can you honestly offer the Lord’s Prayer—“Forgive us as we forgive”?
Luke has it, “Forgive us, for we forgive.”
How can you have the nerve to say this before God when you do not forgive?
It will not do to pray, “Lord, enable us to forgive others.”
That is by no means the language of the Lord’s Prayer.
Reformers are very apt to be deceived by the exercise of partial benevolence.
They mistake hatred of sin for love of souls and love for being in general. They can denounce slavery and slaveholding terribly; so could the devil.
No doubt he abhors it as one of the meanest sins in his kingdom.
It is impossible for him not to hate sin and wickedness.
He cannot love it for its own sake, for there is nothing lovely in it.
He must treat sin and sinners with the utmost contempt, for he is a moral being.
No moral being can truly say, “Evil, be my good.”
It is remarkable that some professed reformers show no mercifulness toward sinners, but would apparently call down curses and vengeance on them instead of blessings.
Until they get a right spirit themselves and really try to improve the moral state of men’s hearts, they will do little to bless mankind.
Until the Temperance Reform took on the Washingtonian character and gave its warm right hand to the drunkard to help him up, it accomplished very little indeed.
Then it took a mighty stride.

When the temperance men lifted their fallen neighbors up out of the gutter, washed and clothed them, and kindly led them forward to take the pledge; when they went to their desolate homes and spread joy in the sad hearts there, and supplied needs long unmet—then it was that men turned in crowds from the path of the destroyer.
I knew of a case in Boston.
In a Methodist meeting one cold winter evening, my friend saw a man slip in at a late hour and lean, shivering with cold, over the stove.
After the service he spoke kindly to the sufferer, who replied with a humble apology for intruding there, and said he hoped he had done no harm.
When questioned, he told a pitiful tale of poverty and sorrow, and revealed that he had been living the life of a miserable drunkard, and that his family was suffering terribly.
My friend said, “I will go home with you”; then he took his arm and went on, stopping at a grocery store to order some provisions sent, and at a coal yard to order some coal.
So with his own arrival came also these welcome and badly needed supplies.
To the poor sufferers in that home of sorrow, his visit seemed like that of an angel of mercy.
His words too and his whole manner were those of kindness.
He said to the father of that family, “I cannot bear to see you drunk ever again.
You must drink no more.
I would rather be whipped until I bleed than see you turn back again to the path of death.”
I mention this case to show you the difference between hunting a man down with justice and following him with mercy.
I have spoken of the difference in relations and duties between the magistrate and the man.
The same difference holds between the citizen and the man.
As a citizen, one may be bound to give information against crime, while as a man, he has no right to avenge himself.
The execution of law aims at the protection of the public.
In view of the public interest, we have no right to refuse to inform against those who destroy property and disturb the peace.
Suppose a villain should come into your house and commit murder there.
You are bound to arrest him and report him to the proper authorities.
The good of other families, exposed to the murderous spirit of such a man, demands it.
But at the same time, you are bound to pray for him and do all you can to bring him to real repentance before God.

You should say to him, “Come now, you have committed an awful crime; I have informed against you, as I was bound to do; but I still love you, and I beg you to repent of your sin and give yourself up to Christ.”
As a private individual, no man may indulge in revenge.
Suppose you have been wronged ever so much; still, if you cannot pray and labor for the reformation and salvation of the one who has wronged you, you are not right before God.
If you cannot rejoice in the prosperity of any human being whatever—if it spoils your happiness to see anyone happy—you are greatly wrong in heart.
This fact shows how impossible it would be for you to enjoy the bliss of heaven if you were there.
Many have a malicious disposition, and seem to love to store up and brood over their grievances with malicious feelings.
Backsliding often begins with grievances that are cherished and not forgiven.
You will find that backsliders are almost always censorious.
They cherish a quarrelsome spirit and go through life elbowing their way along, always at odds with somebody and often with many.
Suppose you die in this state; you surely go to hell!
How dare a man live in a state of unmercifulness toward another!
It is horrible to live like that!
You may die suddenly; you certainly cannot die in peace while that evil spirit of hostility lurks in your heart.
You may have had a quarrel with a neighbor, and are saying, “If he goes to heaven, I don’t want to meet him there.”
If he does go to heaven, you will not meet him there in your present spirit—that is very certain.
But if he goes to hell, you will meet him there!
You cannot go to heaven unless you can forgive everybody, and with a free heart too.
One woman who had a bitter quarrel with another was asked, “What if you were to meet her in the eternal world?”
“I would hunt her down in hell,” was her reply.
“Do you expect to go to hell?”
“I have nothing but the spirit of hell!
It burns and boils in my soul continually.”
Two men, professing Christians, had a quarrel one evening.

The next morning, one said to the other, “We shall love each other better after we have taken a ground-sweat”—as if lying in the grave until the resurrection would sweat off such bitterness of spirit!
No indeed, the grave has no such power.
The “ground-sweat” never does that work.
Nothing but the mercy of Jesus and his dying love can reach this malice of spirit and cure it; and this cure must be worked here on earth.
Are you going to your deathbed with an unforgiving spirit?
Do you say to your enemy, “He has wronged me; I cannot forgive him”?
Oh, what an awful state! Suppose I have to preach your funeral sermon.
Shall I say, “This man has gone to heaven”?
God forbid that I should speak treacherously and deceive the living!
But you say, “I have been so injured and wronged!”
You have? And had Christ not been injured too?
Yet did he not cry, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do”?
Had Stephen not been injured?
Yet hear him pray, “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge!”
This is how men die who are going to heaven.
But you who have no forgiveness in your souls, do not sleep on in your unforgiving spirit.

Go to Jesus; bathe your soul in the tears of repentance until you can offer the Lord’s Prayer without fear that, being forgiven only as you forgive others, you would bring down nothing but curses on your soul!
“And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Matthew 22:39
In speaking on this portion of our Lord’s summary of the divine law, I will first inquire what KIND of love is required here;
Second, state some of the things implied in this love;
Third, show that nothing short of this love is true humanity; and
Lastly, that nothing less is true morality.
I. The love required toward our neighbor is certainly not complacency in his character.
Complacency is approval of and delight in character; but our Lord makes no distinction between the good and the bad, and therefore he requires us to love them all.
But it cannot be that he requires us to approve of and delight in the character of bad men; and so we must conclude that the love of complacency is not in his mind, and is not the thing he requires.
To take complacency in the character of wicked men as wicked is to be as bad as they are.
No reasonable man can suppose this to be what the Savior requires, or what he interprets the law of God to require.
Again, it is not the love of fondness that we sometimes feel toward particular individuals.
Some persons are naturally pleasing to certain other persons; some are pleasing to all, being naturally amiable and suited to awaken pleasant emotions.
But this is not the love referred to in the text.
Again, this love cannot be involuntary.

As I said before of the love required toward God, that it must be a voluntary act and could not be involuntary, because if it were, it could not justly be demanded, so I say of this love to our neighbor.
It cannot be involuntary, for if it were, no just being could require it.
Positively, this love to our neighbor is and must be good will.
God’s love to man is good will—a pure and strong interest in his welfare, a desire for his happiness, and the positive willing of his happiness as the object dearest to his heart.
The way in which his great love has shown itself proves this.
Our very reason affirms that this is the love God has borne and still bears toward our race.
Consequently we must conclude that this is the love he requires men to exercise toward one another.
Note again that this love requires us to value our neighbor’s interests as our own.
This rule applies to all our neighbors—to our enemies as well as to our friends.
Again, it is a constant love, not fitful and fleeting, and not impulsive, but flowing from a fountain of good will that endures forever.
It is a state of mind—an established state that regards our neighbor’s interests as our own.

blocks.x: II. I now pass on to name some things implied in this love.

s: (1.) It does not imply the universal and equal distribution of our energies and means among all mankind, or even among all who may be near enough to be known to us.
It cannot mean to imply this, because with such a meaning it would be impossible to obey it.

There can be no doubt that the law of God demands good will toward all mankind, always and under all circumstances; but there are circumstances that forbid such ways of expressing it as would be proper at other times.

A criminal suffering the just sentence of human law must not receive from us the same acts of good will as would be fitting after his sentence has been served, or if he were not under sentence at all.
The relation that sinners come to hold toward God under the sentence of his law is such that it forbids him to bless them.

It is not that he has ceased to love them in the sense of a deep, intense interest in their happiness; but he loves all the rest of his intelligent creatures no less, and their interests demand of him that he carry out his righteous law against the wicked.
Therefore he cannot give them even so much good as a cup of cold water.
The same circumstances may sometimes demand of us the same withholding of positive efforts to do good to the wicked.
Again, since each one is required by this law to love his neighbor, it is plain that God intends these kind services to be mutual.
If God does us good, we should gratefully seek to do him good.
If he promotes our interests, we should strive to promote his.
So it is with children toward their parents.
Children should not always receive and never give, but should count it a great privilege to repay their parents for the labor and care spent on them.
When parents are spared in life long enough to become old and helpless, their children should rejoice in the opportunity to repay the favors shown to them when they too were helpless.
So it is with subjects and rulers.
So also between pupils and teachers there are mutual interests.
On neither side should it be all receiving and no giving; but there should be mutual receiving and giving on both sides.
In the same way this Institution, including its teachers and its students, stands in close relation to its founders and patrons.
Others have labored; we enter into their labors.
Others have given their money; we are enjoying its benefit.
There is not a building here that is not indebted to some donors from elsewhere.
Others have prayed, and we have received blessings from God for those prayers.
Therefore we should seek to repay those favors, doing all we can to promote the very objects to which those Christian friends have so devoted their wealth and their prayers.
So ministers who preach and their people who hear should be mutually giving and receiving good, to and from one another.
All of us, instead of being merely receivers of good from others, should strive to do good to others also, giving it back generously into their bosom.
Why should this principle not apply to all men toward God?
You who have never cared for God: is it right that you should receive everything from God and make him no return of love and obedience?
Have you no zeal for his honor and no devotion to his interests?
He has nourished and brought you up as a child, and you have done nothing but rebel against him.
Is that right? Why should you not rather say, “God has given me talents, and I must render them back to him in their use as I have opportunity”?
Certainly you must regard God as your neighbor in this sense, that He has interests and rights, and you are under the highest obligation to repay Him for countless favors.
The same is also true of your relations to the church of Jesus Christ.
How much do you owe to Him?
In view of it all, do you have any right to say, “Not one word of acknowledgment, not one thank offering shall he ever have from me!”
What do you not owe him!
Has it ever occurred to you how truly you owe him your very existence, since, but for his mission of mercy, you would never have lived?
But for that offering and sacrifice on Calvary, none of us could have had any existence at all.
But for that, Adam and Eve would have been cut down at once in their sin, the law taking its course of righteous judgment: “In the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.”
You live, therefore, only because God has had mercy on our race.
Come now, step up at once to meet the claims of this great truth.
Are you not indebted to God for everything?
And will you pay back absolutely nothing?
Here you are in the house of God, surrounded by an atmosphere of prayer, instead of being in hell, shrieking and wailing in the depths of despair!
Do you say, “I don’t owe Christ anything”?
But you profess to be respectable.
Yet who can respect you if you treat Jesus Christ this way?
Have you no sympathy with his great sacrifices and sufferings to save you?
Would you leave all the labor and sacrifice to him, and make no response of love or gratitude?
Will you utterly refuse to love him?
Do you say, “He is welcome to love me and to die for me; but I have nothing to pay him in return.
I leave it to him to do and to suffer everything, and not a word of thanks can he have from me”?
Do you think this is right?
Is it generous? Ought it to be considered respectable?
III. Nothing short of the love required here is true humanity.
It is not true humanity to do good only to one’s own offspring.
They are regarded as parts of oneself, and so doing good to them only is nothing more than a slightly enlarged selfishness.
Nothing is really love to man—true humanity—except that love which values human well-being for its intrinsic worth, and loves man as man.
IV. Nothing short of this is true morality.
Nothing less is required by our reason and our conscience.
To lay special stress on our own interests because they are our own is not true morality.
It is not, even though we aim to be honest in seeking the good of particular individuals.
If it is only particular individuals that we love, this is partiality.
Again, no man loves his friends in the sense that pleases God unless he also truly loves his enemies.
Suppose a man does love his friends.
Hear what Jesus Christ says about exactly this case: “If you love those who love you, what reward do you have?”
“Do not even the tax collectors [notorious sinners] do the same?”
Jesus Christ says, “Love your enemies.”
It can never be supposed that anyone does right unless he loves his enemies.
Someone says, “There are certain persons whom I never wrong.”
What is the motive that leads you to do them good and not evil?
If you truly loved your neighbor for right reasons, you would love every neighbor, and you would take every living man for your neighbor in the sense of this law.
You would love every known being, because you would love to promote the happiness of all sentient beings, and you would aim to love each one according to the value of his well-being.
Real benevolence would as truly seek to do good to enemies as to friends, if it could reach them, and do them as much good.
Understand that to love your friend rightly, you must love him as God does, and for the same reasons.
You cannot love him rightly unless you also love your enemies, and for a similar reason.
No man does anything for his friend that is acceptable to God unless he would do as much for his enemies, if he could.
God can give him no credit for doing good to his friends unless he does it on a principle that would make him do as much for his enemies if he could.

No man does any duty acceptably to God for one man while he refuses or willfully neglects to do the same for another; and I base this on the ground that God’s law requires you to love all your neighbors—every neighbor; and if you have the spirit of obedience to God, you will.
No man does right in any proper sense who does not act from universal and disinterested love.
On any other ground it cannot be acceptable for one moment.
That mother nursing her baby has no credit from God for this if she does it on no higher principle than the mere animal.
She is bound to love her own offspring because God has placed her in exactly those relations.
But let her by no means think she has any credit from God for merely obeying her animal instincts.
Her soul should go higher than the mere animal.
She is bound to make it her study to please God.
Nothing short of this can be the condition of salvation.
No man can be out of sin and in grace who has not been brought into a state of true love to his neighbor.
What would become of a man applying at heaven’s gate for admission, who should meet there an enemy—a man he had never loved, whom he had hated and never prayed for?
Could he pass by such a man into heaven?
How could you enjoy heaven without a holy heart?
Some of you would hurry out, as we have sometimes seen rude, ill-mannered boys rush to get out of church even before the services of worship were over.
He who loves his neighbor will understand that it is one of his neighbor’s rights to enjoy the public worship of God without being disturbed.
Without this love, salvation is naturally impossible.
It is governmentally impossible; it cannot be, as long as God rules and cares for the interests of his great kingdom.
The entrance to heaven is so guarded all around that nothing that works abomination shall by any means enter—nothing unholy.
A man going there in his selfishness!
Not if God can keep him out!

blocks.x: REMARKS.

s: If all men obeyed the laws of God, society would be perfect.
I do not mean that there would be no further progress, no advance, no improvement; no, not that, for much remains to be done.
But this is true: morality would be perfect; there would be no more war and strife.
Every family would be a little emblem of heaven.
Every community would bear the image of heaven.
The wings of angels would come down so near that they would fan such loving hearts; and heaven’s doors would stand open all day long before such a people.
We see how we are to treat those who are oppressed and in slavery.
We are to put ourselves in their position and inquire what we would ask them to do for us, in their circumstances.
Suppose that I and my family are in slavery.
An election is coming on.
Do I have a right to expect that my friends in Ohio will cast their votes so as to bear most directly on my liberation?
I would be very inclined to think that no man ought to cast his vote against my liberty for the mere sake of money or office.
Even politicians can see how shameful and how outrageously wrong it is to hold a man as a piece of property.
That this should be considered a Bible institution is of all monstrous things the most monstrous!
It is so revolting that I can hardly imagine how anybody can be honest in holding this opinion.
Yet let us be candid: I can easily see that the merely legal relation may exist without any violation of the law of love.
This golden rule is equally applicable everywhere and in all circumstances.
It is good when applied to the matter of asking favors.
We ought not to ask a favor of any man when a knowledge of his circumstances and a proper sympathy for his welfare, such as we would have him feel for ours, would forbid it.
The same is true of receiving favors.
This law, honestly applied, would show us what favors we should be willing to allow others to do for us.
Sometimes we cannot properly allow others to do us favors.
If a poor man has worked for me a month and refuses to receive payment, I too must by all means refuse to receive his labor as a gift.
A proper regard for his circumstances compels me to refuse so great a gift from him.
He cannot afford to give it; therefore I cannot afford to receive it.
You may see from this subject what the morality of unregenerate men is.
It is not morality at all, in any just sense.
All their morality is only sin.
You may also see God’s personal relations to selfishness.
Every particle of selfishness is personally hostile and hateful to God.
It is so utterly unlike his heart, so totally opposed to all his principles and to all his acts, that he can have no fellowship with it.
He must forever hold it in utter abhorrence.
You may also see his governmental relations to sin.
He can bear the personal insult, and he does—does for the time being, and, but for governmental reasons, would perhaps pass it over forever.
He bears with sinners now; he does not fret; he does not show excited passion, as men do under insult; but the governmental bearings of sin he cannot overlook.
The selfishness of men toward himself and toward one another he must see.
He is a magistrate, bearing the highest responsibilities of the universe.
All eyes are turned on him.
He must mark the iniquities that are done among his subjects and his creatures.
He must see all their wickedness, biting and devouring one another, trampling each other down.
All eyes are lifted up toward him.
What does the Judge of all the earth say to this!
Ah, this must be answered!
God’s relations to his government make it an awful thing for man to love selfishness.
Every selfish sinner is in certain danger of eternal death.
Men know this and cannot help but know it.
God’s mercy flows at your feet, a deep, broad, glorious current; yet you do not heed it!
Yet you thrust Jesus away!
You have done so often and long.
Can you do it still longer?
Jesus, with bleeding heart and loving hand, is pressing near to save you, but you are saying: Depart from me! Let me alone in my sins a while longer!
I will not have this man rule over me, nor save me, on such terms of salvation!
O sinner! Will you still pursue a course so ruinous, and so outrageously abusive to Jesus Christ?
